World.title: Japan Tops Global Waste Index 2025; U.S., Israel, and Chile Rank as Worst Polluters
World.content:
Japan has emerged as the world leader in waste management, while Israel, Chile, and the United States rank among the worst-performing countries, according to the Global Waste Index 2025 released by Slovak-based waste technology company Sensoneo.

The report, which ranks all 38 OECD member states based on their waste generation and disposal practices, highlights significant disparities in global waste management. Sensoneoâs index evaluates countries on per capita waste generation, recycling, incineration, and landfill use.

Israel and Chile ranked last and second-to-last, respectively, primarily due to their heavy reliance on environmentally damaging landfilling practices. Israel sends 524 of the 650 kilograms of waste it generates per person each year directly to landfills. Chile recycles just 1% of its waste and sends more than 95% to landfill.

The United States, which increased its per capita waste generation from 811 to 951 kilograms since 2022, remains the highest generator of municipal solid waste globally. The U.S. disposes of nearly half of that â 447 kilograms â in landfills annually. Neighboring Canada also performed poorly, landfilling 67% of its annual 694 kg per capita waste.

At the other end of the spectrum, Japan ranked No. 1, followed by South Korea and Estonia, all of which combine relatively low waste generation with efficient disposal methods. Japan sends only 3 kilograms per capita to landfill, relying heavily on incineration (245 kg) and maintaining a controlled recycling rate.

European countries dominated the top 10 rankings, with Austria, Germany, Finland, Belgium, Sweden, Norway, and Switzerland all demonstrating strong waste management systems. Austria topped the recycling chart with 334 kilograms of municipal waste recycled per person annually â accounting for 42% of its total waste.

Meanwhile, Spain fell four places to 27th despite minor improvements. The country reduced its landfill and incineration rates slightly while increasing recycling by 10 kilograms per capita. However, its overall waste generation rose by 10 kg compared to the 2022 index.

The index revealed that in 12 of the 38 countries, over half of all waste is still landfilled â including in developed nations like Australia, New Zealand, and Canada. By contrast, Switzerland was the only country to report zero landfill disposal, while Belgium, Finland, Estonia, and Japan landfilled less than 3 kg per person.

Other key findings include:

New Zealand , Finland , and Iceland posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita.

, , and posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita. From an environmental standpoint, incineration is considered preferable to landfilling, but excessive reliance on either suggests a need for stronger waste reduction and recycling strategies.

About the Index and Sensoneo

First launched in 2019, the Global Waste Index is published every three years by Sensoneo, a company specializing in digital transformation for waste management systems. The 2025 edition is based on the latest available national data.

Sensoneo operates in 87 countries and provides waste monitoring solutions to cities, industries, and governments. It is the only company to have successfully implemented deposit return systems (DRS) IT infrastructure in nine countries, achieving recycling rates above 90%.

In Madrid, Sensoneo is deploying 11,100 smart sensors, marking the worldâs largest smart waste monitoring installation to date.

World.title: South Korean Model and Actor Kim Jong Suk Dies at 29, Family Urges Respect Amid Speculation
World.content:
South Korean model and television personality Kim Jong Suk has died at the age of 29, his family confirmed on June 6. The news has shocked fans and colleagues across the countryâs entertainment industry, where Kim rose to prominence following his appearance on tvNâs 2022 reality dating show Skip Dating.

Kim, who began his career in modeling before transitioning to television, had been steadily gaining popularity in recent years. His sudden death has prompted an outpouring of grief and speculation online.

While the exact cause of death remains unconfirmed, some media reports have linked Kimâs passing to an incident in Hanam involving a violent altercation between a young man and his girlfriend. According to the reports, law enforcement responded to the scene, after which the man allegedly died by suicide after jumping from a high-rise building.

Amid widespread online discussion and conjecture, Kimâs family issued a public plea for restraint, asking the public and media to refrain from spreading misinformation or making disrespectful assumptions.

Kimâs older sister posted on social media, expressing the family’s devastation and emotional exhaustion. âWe ask for privacy and understanding during this difficult time,â she wrote, emphasizing the familyâs wish to grieve in peace.

Details regarding funeral arrangements have not been made public.

World.title: Chilean shipping company weighs a monthly route between Punta Arenas and the Falklands
World.content:
Chilean shipping company weighs a monthly route between Punta Arenas and the Falklands

26th Sunday, July 2026 - 09:45 UTC Full article

The visit was organized by the Falkland Islands Development Corporation (FIDC), the territory's economic development body

Chilean company Easter Island Naviera (EIL) is considering establishing a monthly cargo shipping service between Punta Arenas and the Falklands, following a visit to the archipelago in which its representatives held around a dozen meetings with local businesses and presented the project to the Islands' chamber of commerce.

The visit was organized by the Falkland Islands Development Corporation (FIDC), the territory's economic development body. According to the information released, the company would finalize its business plan and could launch the service if follow-up on those contacts confirms sufficient interest from the local private sector.

“There is clearly an interest from Chile in re-establishing a commercial maritime connection with the Falkland Islands. Easter Island Naviera's visit and the positive response from the business community show the seriousness with which this project is being pursued,” said Sam Cockwell, strategic projects manager at the FIDC.

The body's chief executive, Zachary Franklin, credited the progress to commercial exchanges over the past two years. “The visit of a business delegation from Chile, and the visit of the FIDC-led delegation to Punta Arenas and Santiago, significantly helped turn this simple 'good idea' into a real opportunity,” he said. The FIDC has developed those contacts in collaboration with the British Chamber of Commerce in Chile, with reciprocal delegations during 2024 and 2025.

Beyond identifying what cargo Island businesses are looking to ship through Chile, the company also examined options for exporting materials to that country, including scrap metal. Easter Island Naviera currently provides logistical and maritime support between mainland Chile and Rapa Nui, as well as cargo services from Valparaíso to other parts of the country.

The archipelago already maintains commercial links with Chile. Airline LATAM operates the air connection between Punta Arenas and the Mount Pleasant base, and food, fishery products, and various supplies arrive from the mainland.

Several Argentine media outlets linked the initiative to the advance of the oil project in the North Falkland Basin and to the supply of energy infrastructure, although the statements released by the FIDC and the company refer to a commercial connection of a general nature.

The project emerges at a moment of diplomatic friction in the South Atlantic. In recent weeks, Argentina's Foreign Ministry lodged a formal protest with London over the movements of the British patrol vessel HMS Medway, which the United Kingdom attributed to a routine logistics mission, and voiced displeasure at the participation of Chilean Navy personnel in protocol activities during the ship's call at Punta Arenas.

World.title: Brazilian industry estimates nearly half its US exports will face additional tariffs
World.content:
Brazilian industry estimates nearly half its US exports will face additional tariffs

25th Saturday, July 2026 - 12:39 UTC Full article

The study, released on Thursday, details that the new 12.5% rate reaches 4,060 Brazilian products

Some 48.7% of Brazilian exports bound for the United States will be subject to some form of additional tariff following the entry into force of the new forced-labor levy, according to a study by the National Confederation of Industry (CNI), the country's main industrial employers' body.

The study, released on Thursday, details that the new 12.5% rate reaches 4,060 Brazilian products. Of those, 3,985 were already subject to the 25% surcharge in force since Wednesday and will now pay a total of 37.5% to enter the US market. That group accounts for 80.7% of affected exports, some $10.8 billion. Another 75 products, worth $1.6 billion, will be covered only by the new rate. Together, the measure covers $12.4 billion, equivalent to 29.4% of Brazilian sales to that destination.

The new levies stem from the investigation conducted under Section 301 of US trade law, which covered 60 trading partners. In its final determination, the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) included Brazil among the countries that, in its assessment, “failed to impose and effectively enforce a ban” on the import of goods produced with forced labor.

The CNI challenged that rationale. According to the confederation, the justifications presented by the USTR do not reflect Brazilian reality, since the country has some of the most advanced legislation to prevent and eradicate forced labor across supply chains, with internationally recognized mechanisms for inspection, accountability, and worker protection.

“It is essential that dialogue between Brazil and the United States be maintained and deepened. At the same time, we need to act quickly to soften the impact on the affected companies,” the body's president, Ricardo Alban, said in a statement, adding that they are holding talks with the federal government and with the most affected sectors to define short-term measures.

The Brazilian government called the tariffs improper and signaled a response. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva said the country would not sit lamenting the measure and announced a credit line for the sectors involved.

Brazil ended up in the highest band of the new scheme, while Argentina secured the minimum 10% rate through commitments made in its bilateral agreement with Washington to ban such imports. The tariff round, covering about 99% of US imports, was applied under a different instrument from the levies the Supreme Court struck down in February, when it found the administration had exceeded its authority by invoking an emergency powers law.

World.title: Goldman Sachs cuts Argentina's growth forecast to 2.7% and looks ahead to the elections
World.content:
Goldman Sachs cuts Argentina's growth forecast to 2.7% and looks ahead to the elections

25th Saturday, July 2026 - 09:22 UTC Full article

Despite the revision, the bank considered that the economy is “expanding at a moderate pace” and maintained a favorable assessment of several aspects of the economic program

Goldman Sachs lowered its growth forecast for Argentina's economy in 2026 from 3% to 2.7% and anticipated a possible contraction in activity during the second quarter, according to a report by the bank. The institution also said economic performance will increasingly be assessed against the presidential elections of October 2027.

The cut followed April and May indicators that came in below expectations. In the first quarter, gross domestic product had grown 0.7% on a seasonally adjusted basis, an improvement the report attributed to the statistical carryover from late 2025 and to March's performance, which offset weaker figures for January and February.

Despite the revision, the bank considered that the economy is “expanding at a moderate pace” and maintained a favorable assessment of several aspects of the economic program. It highlighted the commitment to fiscal balance, reserve accumulation, and an improving trade position: by its calculations, the central bank has bought close to $13 billion so far this year and net reserves have risen by around $6.6 billion. The 12-month trade surplus reached the equivalent of 3.2% of output, with the energy sector accounting for nearly half of the result.

The bank also praised the disinflation process. After the 1.9% recorded in June, it projected that prices will continue to decelerate in the second half and that the year will close near 29%. In its overall assessment it said the country remains “on the right track in terms of macroeconomic policy,” while warning that political and social challenges persist. “The margin for error is narrow,” it said, anticipating greater investor attention on Javier Milei's prospects for reelection.

Goldman Sachs's forecast sits below other recent estimates. Moody's projects growth of 3.4% for 2026 and 3.5% for 2027, while the International Monetary Fund estimates 3.5% this year and 4% next.

The report came days after Moody's raised Argentina's sovereign rating to B3 from Caa1, with a positive outlook, the third upgrade in under three months following those by Fitch and Standard & Poor's. It is the first time in a decade that the three main agencies have aligned their assessments. The central bank exceeded $10 billion in foreign-currency purchases in the first half, meeting the target agreed with the multilateral lender.

Country risk, meanwhile, closed the week at 437 basis points after rising 4.3%, with a session high of 445. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva is scheduled to visit the country next week.

World.title: New US tariff scheme expands Argentine zero-duty lines to 2,212
World.content:
New US tariff scheme expands Argentine zero-duty lines to 2,212

25th Saturday, July 2026 - 09:14 UTC Full article

Argentina was also placed in the lowest band of the new regime, with an additional 10% tariff, the same rate that previously applied

The new US tariff scheme that took effect on Friday raised to 2,212 the number of Argentine tariff lines that can enter the US market at a 0% rate. To the 1,675 lines already covered by the Reciprocal Trade and Investment Agreement (ARTI), signed on February 5 in Washington, another 537 were added following a review by the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR).

Argentina was also placed in the lowest band of the new regime, with an additional 10% tariff, the same rate that previously applied. Under the criteria published by the USTR, that rate applies to economies that already ban the import of goods produced with forced labor, committed to doing so through a reciprocal trade agreement, or apply a partial regime with that effect. That group also includes Canada, Mexico, India, Indonesia, the United Kingdom, Guatemala, and Honduras, among others. The remaining partners covered received a 12.5% rate.

In Argentina's case, its placement in the lower band rests on the commitments made in the February agreement to ban such imports, even though the domestic regime is not yet in force. The original 1,675 lines, which official estimates suggest would enable exports worth some $1.013 billion, were not affected by the new mechanism. A further 93 country-specific exemptions were added, including jojoba and argan oils, live animals, flowers, cork, timber, and precious stones.

The US Chamber of Commerce in Argentina (AmCham) said the ARTI will begin to be fully implemented and that the measure broadens opportunities for local exports. The Argentine government, for its part, played down the impact of the new regime and prefers to await definitions from Washington before sending the bilateral agreement to Congress for consideration.

Analysts quoted by the Argentine press nonetheless pointed to elements of uncertainty. International relations scholar Julieta Zelicovich said the tariffs work as “a pressure mechanism” that creates a “state of permanent negotiation” with trading partners, and anticipated that the new rules will be challenged in court, as happened with the tariffs issued under the emergency powers law and Section 122. Economist Federico Vaccarezza warned that the agreement lacks a dispute settlement mechanism.

The round covers 60 trading partners accounting for about 99% of US imports and replaces the universal 10% tariff that expired on Friday. Brazil, by contrast, has since Wednesday faced 25% duties issued under the same legal instrument, following a separate investigation.

World.title: Uruguay: nearly half of those polled say the government is falling short of expectations
World.content:
Uruguay: nearly half of those polled say the government is falling short of expectations

25th Saturday, July 2026 - 09:10 UTC Full article

The same poll put Orsi's approval at 24% and disapproval at 56%, his worst reading since taking office

For 49% of Uruguayans surveyed, Yamandú Orsi's government is performing below the expectations they held at the start of the administration, according to the latest poll by the consultancy Factum, covering the third two-month period of 2026. The study, with fieldwork conducted between June 2 and 20 and released by VTV Noticias, shows a sustained deterioration in perceptions of the government since the beginning of the term.

Among the remaining respondents, 27% consider that the government is performing as they expected and just 1% believe it is exceeding their expectations. Another 22% said they expected nothing from the current administration, and 1% declined to answer.

Comparison with earlier measurements shows the scale of the shift. In the fourth period of 2025, 45% rated the government's performance as equal to or above their expectations, against 30% who placed it below. In the third period of 2026 that relationship reversed: 28% now place it at or above, and nearly half below.

By region, the negative assessment is slightly higher in the country's interior, where 50% consider the government to be falling short of expectations, against 49% in Montevideo. Favorable views, by contrast, are somewhat higher in the capital: 31% of Montevideo residents rate the government as equal to or better than expected, a figure that drops to 25% in the interior.

The most critical age group is the youngest. Among people aged 18 to 33, 50% believe the government is below their expectations and only 18% place it at or above. Those over 62 show the relatively most favorable assessment, with 35% rating the government as equal to or better than expected, though 44% also place it below.

The sharpest differences emerge when 2024 voting is taken into account. Among those who voted for the Frente Amplio, the governing coalition, 52% say the administration is falling short of what they expected, while just 3% say they expected nothing from it.

The expectations measure is not equivalent to an approval rating, as it compares the government's performance with what each person anticipated at the start of the term. On that separate question, the same poll put Orsi's approval at 24% and disapproval at 56%, his worst reading since taking office, with a cumulative drop of 13 points since the first period of the year. The fieldwork coincided with the controversy over the purchase of an official vehicle.

World.title: Trump jokes about a third term at correspondents' dinner, three months after the attack
World.content:
Trump jokes about a third term at correspondents' dinner, three months after the attack

25th Saturday, July 2026 - 09:06 UTC Full article

The evening was a repeat of the April 25 event, which was interrupted when a man tried to force his way through a security checkpoint and fired near the ballroom

US President Donald Trump joked about the possibility of seeking a third term during his speech at the annual White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA) dinner, held on Friday in Washington. Toward the end of his roughly hour-long remarks, he put on a hat reading “Trump 2028.” The 22nd Amendment to the US Constitution bars a president from serving more than two terms.

The evening was a repeat of the April 25 event, which was interrupted when a man tried to force his way through a security checkpoint and fired near the ballroom. The accused was subdued by officers before reaching the venue and faces charges over the incident. The rescheduled edition was held at the Waldorf Astoria hotel — which Trump owned before his first presidency — with a considerably smaller guest list and heightened security.

“As I said three months ago, the show must go on,” the president said at the outset, in his first appearance as president at an event he had avoided for years. Trump said he had scrapped the harshest passages of the speech he had prepared for April. “That was going to be a doozy,” he said.

Through his remarks he praised part of the press corps and criticized other journalists, while taking swipes at political rivals and public figures, among them hosts Jimmy Kimmel and Jimmy Fallon, Representative Ilhan Omar, California Governor Gavin Newsom, former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, and musician Bruce Springsteen. Several comments referred to the physical appearance or intellect of those mentioned, and in one case he repeated a claim about a congresswoman that was debunked years ago. NPR judged that some of the remarks flirted with racism.

Much of the humor drew a limited response. According to accounts by CNN and The Washington Post, several jokes were met with silence from the audience. His press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, had previewed the speech as “unifying yet vicious, and serious yet hilarious.”

The association's outgoing president, Weijia Jiang, opened the evening with a reference to the April attack, which she said “tested all of us.” The event also featured the annual journalism awards and a tribute to a Secret Service agent who helped subdue the assailant.

Trump, who has maintained a tense relationship with the press throughout his political career, said he respects most of the correspondents and called his attendance an “honor.” He added that he expects to attend next year's edition, in 2027, though he jokingly made his participation conditional on how the media treat him.

World.title: Uruguay faces a 12.5% US tariff as its foreign ministry weighs the implications
World.content:
Uruguay faces a 12.5% US tariff as its foreign ministry weighs the implications

24th Friday, July 2026 - 07:05 UTC Full article

Sources at the Foreign Ministry confirmed the decision and said its implications are being analyzed, while noting that the outcome “was within expectations”

Uruguay was placed in the highest band of the new US tariff scheme, with an additional 12.5% levy on its exports to the United States, for not having an explicit ban on the import of goods produced with forced labor. The measure, which took effect on Friday, raises the rate that had applied to the country since February, of 10%.

Sources at the Foreign Ministry confirmed the decision and said its implications are being analyzed, while noting that the outcome “was within expectations,” given that the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) had announced the start of the investigation in March and released its proposal in June. The Ministry of Economy and Finance confirmed the move from 10% to 12.5%.

The new scheme, applied under Section 301 of US trade law, covers 60 trading partners accounting for about 99% of US imports, and replaces the 10% universal tariff that expired on Friday. Under the USTR's determination, the 12.5% rate applies to economies that have not adopted a ban on the import of goods produced with forced labor, did not commit to implementing one through a reciprocal trade agreement, and are not part of the differentiated calculation group, which includes the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and Switzerland.

The breakdown leaves Uruguay at a disadvantage relative to several regional partners. Argentina, Ecuador, Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador fell under the lower 10% rate, having adopted restrictions or committed to doing so. Costa Rica, Panama, and the Dominican Republic, by contrast, face 12.5%, as does Uruguay. Brazil, meanwhile, has since Wednesday been subject to 25% tariffs issued under the same legal instrument, following a separate investigation.

“The United States has had a forced labor import ban for nearly a century, and rigorously enforces it; it's well past time for our trading partners to do the same,” said US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in announcing the measure.

The USTR said certain products are exempt, among them raw materials whose higher cost could cause supply shortages in the US market, though it did not publish a detailed list. China does not appear in this scheme, as it is subject to separate and higher tariffs.

The round is part of Donald Trump's administration's effort to rebuild its tariff structure after the Supreme Court struck down in February the tariffs issued under an emergency powers law, finding that the administration had exceeded its authority.

World.title: Six candidates to lead the UN debate in the General Assembly with no clear front-runner
World.content:
Six candidates to lead the UN debate in the General Assembly with no clear front-runner

24th Friday, July 2026 - 07:00 UTC Full article

The common thread across the interventions was the need to restore the credibility of an organization facing financial strains and largely absent from negotiations over the world's major conflicts

The six contenders to succeed António Guterres at the head of the United Nations set out their proposals on Thursday in a debate held in the General Assembly Hall, a week before the formal start of the selection process. For nearly two hours they answered questions from diplomats, UN staff, and civil society representatives, in a publicly broadcast session.

The candidates are former Chilean president Michelle Bachelet, former Ecuadorian foreign minister María Fernanda Espinosa, Argentina's Rafael Grossi, currently director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency, Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan, secretary-general of the UN Conference on Trade and Development, former Guyanese foreign minister Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, and former Senegalese president Macky Sall. Five of the six come from Latin America and the Caribbean, in line with the regional rotation expectation that favors the region this cycle; Sall is the only African candidate. Guterres leaves office on December 31.

The common thread across the interventions was the need to restore the credibility of an organization facing financial strains and largely absent from negotiations over the world's major conflicts. “I would like no one to ask me again where the UN is. That will be my indicator,” Grynspan said when asked what achievements she would hope to show after five years. On Security Council paralysis, she argued that “the blockade of the Security Council is when the job of the secretary-general starts,” citing her role in the deal that allowed grain exports through the Black Sea as a precedent applicable to the Strait of Hormuz crisis.

Bachelet stressed the importance of the post's moral authority and said neutrality and independence are essential for all 193 member states to feel represented. Asked how he would act if a permanent Council member waged a war of aggression, Grossi replied that the secretary-general must “dialogue and listen” and approach conflicts realistically, examining their root causes and the situation of the party under attack. Espinosa said the organization is in crisis and must recover its capacity to prevent conflicts, while Sall focused on reforming the international financial architecture and Rodrigues-Birkett defended the scope for action despite the post's lack of executive power.

The format, with no direct exchange between participants, limited the contrast of ideas. According to analyst Richard Gowan, Grossi is the most frequently mentioned front-runner, though he has not locked up the race, and both Grynspan and Rodrigues-Birkett have significant backing. Several capitals have yet to define their positions. The decisive phase begins on July 30, when the fifteen members of the Security Council, five of them with veto power, start their closed-door voting.

World.title: The men’s World Cup is over, now Mexico’s women are ready for their moment
World.content:
With the 2026 edition of the men’s World Cup behind us — in which Mexico became the first country to host the sporting event on three separate occasions (1970, 1986 and 2026), leaving an indelible impression on fans worldwide who openly celebrated Mexico’s culture, gastronomy and spirited fandom — the “summer of North American soccer” is coming to a close. Well, sort of. It’s not completely over.

Luckily for fans of fútbol (also known as fút or balompié in Mexico), on-pitch action will resume with a different set of national heroes, as Mexico and the rest of the globe prepare for the upcoming 2027 Women’s World Cup.

World Cup qualifying has already begun

View this post on Instagram A post shared by FOX Sports MX (@foxsportsmx)

Though the tournament won’t actually take place until next summer — hosted in Brazil, marking the first time the FIFA women’s edition will take place on Latin American soil since debuting in 1991 — the race for the trophy is already underway.

Last winter, World Cup qualifying games began; this fall, North American qualifiers, which determine which teams from the region will compete in the World Cup, will conclude.

Here’s a look at Mexico’s national women’s squad and how they have fared so far on their historically arduous journey for sporting glory.

A history of women’s professional soccer in Mexico

Like all women’s sports around the globe, Mexico’s Liga MX Femenil is relatively new and lags behind its male counterpart league in terms of financial support, national investment, media coverage and, as a result, fandom. Despite those barriers, it has been celebrated as a highly successful effort.

The league was announced in late 2016 and officially played its first game in 2017. Since then, it has quietly developed into one of the world’s leading women’s leagues, with the Associated Press reporting that “women’s pro soccer is thriving in Mexico” and The New York Times citing it as the most-watched women’s league on the planet.

That said, it hasn’t been a path without systemic and cultural resistance. Instances of gender bias, sexism and a massive gap in pay and resources have endured. Last summer, Mexican men’s national team legend and former superstar Javier “Chicharito” Hernández was fined by the Mexican Football Federation for demeaning comments on social media that portrayed women as “failing” and “eradicating masculinity,” prompting a response from President Claudia Sheinbaum. In 2023, former Club América Femenil player Scarlett Camberos chose to leave the team and country due to excessive sexual harassment and cyberstalking.

Liga MX Femenil and the birth of the FIFA Women’s World Cup

Though Liga MX Femenil — both its successes and its accentuated reminder of Mexico’s machismo — is relatively nascent, pro women’s soccer in Mexico can be traced back to 1970. Before FIFA’s involvement, an unofficial Women’s World Cup existed as a series of international events independently sponsored by various nations. In those times, Mexico finished in third place at the 1970 World Cup in Italy and ended as runner-up in the largely erased 1971 World Cup in Mexico. It is estimated that the 1971 final at Estadio Azteca drew 110,000 fans. Unofficial tournaments continued throughout the 1980s under non-FIFA-sanctioned entities like the Chinese Taipei Football Association.

Pressure for an official FIFA Women’s World Cup mounted, crescendoing in 1986 when Norwegian delegate Ellen Wille famously urged FIFA to legitimize a women’s tournament in a speech that “changed the course of women’s football,” according to the BBC. In 1988, FIFA organized a trial tournament, the FIFA Women’s Invitation Tournament in China. Overwhelming success resulted in the debut of the official Women’s World Cup in 1991 in China.

Surprisingly, since the FIFA era of the World Cup began, Mexico’s women’s team hasn’t shown much promise. That is finally changing.

The road to the 2027 World Cup is off to a perfect start

In February, Mexico’s women’s team kicked off its World Cup campaign in the preliminary qualifying rounds of the Concacaf W Championship. Concacaf is the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football, representing one of FIFA’s six continental governing bodies, which divides competition into regional tournaments that funnel teams into the World Cup every four years. Under this format, all North American, Central American and Caribbean teams face off, with the four quarterfinal winners earning direct berths to the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup in Brazil.

Currently, Mexico is among the remaining eight North American countries with a chance to secure a World Cup ticket this year. It can do so by defeating Haiti on Nov. 28 at Texas Health Mansfield Stadium in Texas.

Mexico’s women haven’t reached a World Cup since 2015. Unlike the Mexican men’s national team — which has qualified 18 times dating back to 1930 — the women have appeared only three times (1999, 2011 and 2015). While the Women’s World Cup has taken place only nine times compared to 23 for the men, El Tri Femenil has struggled to assert regional dominance, holding a 33.3% qualification rate compared to the men’s nearly 80% rate over a much longer period.

A thus-far ‘flawless’ qualifying journey

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Concacaf W (@concacafw)

However, this World Cup cycle is proving to be different: Mexico’s women have been perfect in their qualifying run, an unprecedented feat. In 2023, Mexico also went undefeated for the first time at the Pan American Games in Santiago, Chile, en route to claiming its first gold medal, proving this current team’s success is no fluke.

El Tri has topped Group A of the Concacaf W Championship qualifiers with a flawless 12 points — going unbeaten in four matches and scoring 36 goals while conceding zero. That places them among the continent’s strongest units and makes them favorites to advance. While they have primarily played lower-ranked competition — such as Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, which Mexico defeated 14-0, and Puerto Rico — the core of the 2023 Pan American Games roster remains intact, leading many to consider this the best women’s team Mexico has ever fielded.

‘The Sorceress’ and other Mexico stars to watch

The roster is headlined by Lizbeth “La Maga” Ovalle (whose nickname translates to “The Sorceress”). Having debuted professionally in 2017, the winger — originally from Aguascalientes, who gained fame as one of Mexico’s top scorers with Tigres UANL — set a record in 2025 by signing a US $1.5 million contract with the Orlando Pride of the National Women’s Soccer League, making it one of the most lucrative deals in women’s soccer history. That same year, Ovalle won the FIFA Marta Award for “Best Goal of the Year” at The Best FIFA Football Awards ceremony for her spectacular “scorpion kick” goal.

Behind Ovalle, Mexico boasts a depth of experience and skill with team captain Rebeca Bernal and the formidable striker Charlyn Corral, one of Mexico’s all-time leading goal scorers. Complementing the veteran leadership is “Concacaf Best Young Player” award winner Alice Soto, a 19-year-old dynamic midfielder who debuted professionally at age 13 and has been scoring in Liga MX Femenil ever since.

Why upcoming qualification matters

Against Haiti, Mexico can automatically claim a direct spot in the 2027 World Cup. A loss would send the team to a playoff round for a second chance.

Haiti is coming off its inaugural appearance in the 2023 Women’s World Cup in Australia and New Zealand. Les Grenadières, as they are known, are a rising team led by attacking duo Melchie Dumornay and Nérilia Mondésir, supported by a defense that has allowed only one goal during qualifiers.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mente Mujer (@mentemujer_)

Though the Women’s World Cup does not begin until next June, the matches will stream on Netflix for the first time, with Mexico’s women primed for their deepest run in tournament history. Furthermore, the 2031 Women’s World Cup will be co-hosted by Mexico, the United States, Costa Rica and Jamaica, marking the first time Mexico will host the FIFA women’s event.

Until then, El Tri Femenil hopes to deliver the nation its first World Cup trophy — regardless of gender.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: US crimes against Mexico from an immigrant’s perspective
World.content:
There is nothing like living outside of your native country to make you reflect on the meaning of its actions, especially if your native country happens to be the United States of America.

Living in Mexico, of course, makes you an automatic representative of your country. This is not a fair position to be in, but it is the story of immigrants everywhere. For the most part, I benefit from my country of origin: whereas plenty of people in the U.S. might look down on an immigrant from Mexico, here it is the opposite. Most people expect me to be cool and interesting, and maybe a little sneaky, scary or both.

We may all be individuals, but the human brain only has so much capacity to think of people as individuals. Gather too many foreign individuals into the same place, and the borders between us blur and blend until we are collectively “others.”

Proud and ashamed

Many things about the U.S. make me very, very proud to be from there: like jazz music, the advancement of civil rights and feminism. First in flight. Customer service agents who are mostly empowered to actually help you. Clean public restrooms with toilet paper, for free!

Other aspects of my home country, however, make me feel deeply, deeply ashamed. A less-than-stellar record when it comes to genocide and enslavement, for example. And oh, Lord, influential religious leaders who would love to send us back to those “good old days.” Deliver us!

When it comes to current events, our treatment of immigrants is at the top of my list right now.

In case you have been protecting your peace more than I have and have abstained from the news, here is a sad summary: Donald Trump returned to office with as much of a mandate as you could suppose to reduce the “out of control” immigration in the U.S.

The killing of innocents and deportation of US citizens

More Latinos in the U.S. than ever voted for him. Strangely, they seemed to believe his promise that he would only target and deport “the criminals” among them. Who would not get behind that?

As it turns out, there are a lot fewer “immigrant criminals” than most people thought. So, unfortunately for the law-abiders, the net was pretty much immediately cast much, much wider to meet detention quotas set by the administration. It caught mothers and fathers taking their children to school. It caught lots and lots of people here legally, papers be damned. It caught those who were brought as children and have known no other life than that of an American.

On top of the generalized horror of being torn from one’s life, there is the very suspicious fact that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has been extremely cagey, caught in lies more than once. It is a fight every time a local official wants to enter a (privately run) detention facility. Those who have come out of them have described the places as unfit for human beings. Rotting food, freezing temperatures and medical needs that are ignored. It is not hard to imagine how over 50 people have died since detentions were ramped up upon Trump’s return, some by suicide. Seventeen of these deaths have been of Mexican nationals (14 in custody, three during “operations”).

A lack of institutional control

Then, of course, there are the vehicle stops and shootings under extremely suspicious circumstances. One of the latest, of course, was that of a Mexican national, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, who turned out not to even be ICE’s target. ICE’s story is that he tried to “weaponize his vehicle” against them. Witnesses say it was quite the opposite. The feds had to be blocked from deporting the witnesses. Weird behavior from an institution that has nothing to hide, right?

In short, things are truly out of control.

The U.S. and Mexico are supposed to be allies. What is going on here?

‘A general lack of accountability’

The main thing that is going on, I believe, is that the wrong people are in charge. Unhappy people voted them in, believing their lies about what the source of their unhappiness actually stemmed from. A threadbare social safety net paired with barely-there labor laws that are happy to let people simply fall through the net and onto the concrete pavement? Nah, that cannot be it … transgender people and immigrants, that is who is hurting you!

Social media — what was supposed to bring us together — and a general lack of accountability to the truth that the internet age has wrought have been excellent at getting people all riled up for stupid reasons.

The U.S. is really pushing it with Mexico right now.

Can Mexico do anything about it?

I personally think that is doubtful, but who knows? I have been wrong before. But if ICE cannot even be held accountable for its on-camera killings of U.S. citizens, who is going to put a boot on its neck over immigrant killings?

And when the offending country has been essentially in charge of international justice for decades, it is hard to tap the brakes. After all, who do you go to for help when the police themselves are corrupt?

Mexico, of course, understands this conundrum in a literal sense. But Mexico also does not claim to be the distributor of justice for the world, either.

Of all the words I might use to describe Mexicans, “proud” would be in the top five. While it seems that a few insults here and there will always be tolerated because of the particular power dynamic the two countries have, you cannot just start letting its citizens die and not even apologize for it.

Mexico files criminal complaints

Claudia Sheinbaum, thankfully, is not letting this go. Criminal complaints, cease-and-desist letters to the private companies in charge of detention, the United Nations. They are going at it from all angles.

The Secretariat of Foreign Affairs is “filing a criminal complaint against whoever is responsible.”

But, gosh. “Whoever is responsible.” Hmm. There is our first issue right there.

Would that be the president, for insisting that as many immigrants be tossed out of the U.S. as possible? Stephen Miller, the architect of the whole thing? Agency heads? Those who hire and “train” (or don’t) ICE officers? The private companies who feel no need to provide adequate living conditions? The offending/negligent immigration officers themselves? It truly is a long list of candidates.

The known reality, of course, is that in the end, it is unlikely anyone will be held to account. I mean, we cannot even get the U.S. to acknowledge that it dropped a bomb on an Iranian girls’ school, killing hundreds of children. Sanctity of life, indeed.

‘The twin monsters of incompetence and cruelty’

How are we supposed to get anyone who has been given “free rein” to carry out the president’s signature plan to play fair?

One of the biggest crimes that humans commit against each other is allowing the twin monsters of incompetence and cruelty to go on … and right now, those twin monsters have the full backing of the U.S. federal government.

This is what happens when you remove the shackles of accountability from institutions filled with the kinds of people who see the world as a fight between those who hunt and those who get hunted.

And many people who work in ICE fancy themselves hunters; they like to prey on people who are running or scared, or just trying to stay out of trouble’s way. They are hunted by the same types of people who used to catch (and torture) runaway slaves. They sniff out fear and relish the capture.

So here we are, many of us, living in a country that has welcomed us in ways that the U.S. would not dream of welcoming our neighbors. It is a strange and sad position to be in. It is also worth remembering that the tables could always turn.

We are the “others” here, after all.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: World Cup glow fades as tariffs and security challenges take center stage
World.content:
This week marked the end of the 2026 FIFA World Cup and the conclusion of Mexico’s third turn as a host country. The week opened with President Sheinbaum’s attendance at the World Cup final in New Jersey, where brief exchanges with Trump, Carney and other officials set the tone for USMCA review talks that resumed in Mexico City. Sheinbaum later called the tournament a diplomatic success, and world leaders had high praise for Mexico’s performance as a host nation.

As World Cup excitement faded, security stories dominated elsewhere. Zacatecas authorities linked the multihomicide of 10 people, including a former mayor, to extortion and official collusion, while a Sinaloa Cartel kingpin, “El Mayo” Zambada, was sentenced to life in prison in the U.S. While El Mayo’s court case has run its course, infighting within the cartel he once led prompted 900 more troops to deploy to Mazatlán, Sinaloa. The week ended with the annoucement of sweeping U.S. sanctions against an opposing organized crime syndicate, the Jalisco New Generation Cartel.

On the economic front, inflation fell to its lowest level since 2020 and a new round of U.S. tariffs largely spared Mexico.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Security: Homicides fall, but high-profile violence persists

México state’s homicide rate has dropped to its lowest level in 19 years, officials said Wednesday, citing a “unified command” strategy that cut daily killings by 58% since September 2024. In Morelos, Governor Margarita González’s administration touted a 54% homicide drop alongside improving public perceptions of safety, even as the state investigated the murder of a mayor with alleged ties to organized crime.

That progress contrasted with events in Sinaloa and Oaxaca. The Zacatecas multihomicide, which included a former mayor of Sombrerete and two Fresnillo officials, is being investigated as a possible case of extortion and collusion between criminals and public officials. In Mazatlán, a string of targeted attacks over the past two weeks left at least a dozen dead, prompting the arrival of 900 additional troops, bringing the security deployment to more than 1,300 personnel. Authorities attributed the violence to the ongoing feud between Sinaloa Cartel factions that intensified after Zambada’s 2024 arrest. Separately, journalist Alejandro Leyva was shot dead in Oaxaca on Wednesday, the second journalist killed in Mexico in less than a week. Federal prosecutors took over the case at the request of state officials.

On Thursday, the U.S. Treasury sanctioned 39 individuals and 16 companies linked to the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, including the CJNG’s new leader, Juan Carlos Valencia González, a.k.a. “El Pelón.” The U.S. called it the largest action ever taken against the group, and Mexico’s financial intelligence unit blocked the same accounts.

El Mayo’s sentencing and its aftermath

Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, Sinaloa Cartel co-founder, was sentenced to life in prison and ordered to forfeit $15 billion by a U.S. federal judge on Monday. In court, Zambada urged young people to avoid a life of crime. President Sheinbaum said she agreed with the sentiment but declined to explicitly endorse a message from a convicted trafficker. Mexican officials said Wednesday it remains unclear whether Zambada could ever be transferred to a Mexican prison, a decision that depends on whether the Attorney General’s Office pursues extradition.

Trade and economy: Inflation eases, tariff fights continue

Mexico’s annual inflation rate fell to 3.10% in the first half of July, the lowest for any comparable period since December 2020, driven largely by falling produce prices. Meanwhile, the tariffs Mexico implemented this year on countries without free trade agreements — chiefly targeting China — cut affected imports by 23.2% between January and May, even as overall imports from Asia rose on surging Taiwanese semiconductor purchases.

On the U.S. side, President Trump’s re-imposed tariffs took effect Friday on dozens of countries, but Mexico avoided major new costs: About 80% of Mexican exports remain tariff-free under the USMCA, according to Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard. While dozens of other countries faced increased tariffs, Mexico’s rate remained at 10%. The U.S. gave Mexico a heads-up before the announcement, as U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer visited Mexico City this week to meet with Sheinbaum and press for stricter automotive rules of origin in the ongoing USMCA review, citing a growing U.S. auto trade deficit with Mexico.

Health, migration and infrastructure

Deputy Health Minister Eduardo Clark reported that 30 public hospital projects have been completed since October 2024, adding 1,474 beds toward a goal of 9,000 by 2030, with 33 more projects due this year. Health officials also moved to calm fears over a U.S. Cyclospora outbreak initially attributed to lettuce from Guanajuato: After the FDA retracted a positive test result, Mexican authorities said there was no evidence of contamination in Mexican-grown produce.

A new report from the Migration Policy Institute found the Mexican-born population in the U.S. has fallen to 11.1 million, down more than 500,000 since a 2007 peak, a decline researchers said could accelerate amid stepped-up immigration enforcement. On infrastructure, the government launched the second construction phase of its passenger rail program, which will link central Mexico to Saltillo and the Pacific coast, while separate data showed Mexico is drawing more international tourists but earning less per visitor as land-crossing traffic outpaces higher-spending air arrivals.

Also this week, the federal government joined Jalisco state officials in announcing a joint effort to rehabilitate Guadalajara’s aging water infrastructure and curb industrial contamination of the Lerma River, while Mexico City announced three regional forums to debate social media and AI regulation for minors.

Looking ahead

USMCA negotiations are set to continue following this week’s talks with Greer, with both sides aiming for interim agreements before year’s end even as the review process stretches toward 2036. Security officials face pressure to build on regional and national homicide declines while containing the Sinaloa Cartel factional violence driving unrest in Mazatlán and elsewhere. Investigations into the Zacatecas multihomicide and the killing of journalist Alejandro Leyva remain open, with federal authorities now involved in both cases.

World.title: Postcards from Mexico: On the Cabo San Lucas Marina
World.content:
CABO SAN LUCAS, Baja California Sur, Oct. 25 — It’s quiet and cool off the strip. The abarrotes are just opening, and there’s an old man in a vest up the block pushing a shopping cart full of empty beer cans. That might be mop-up duty from last night’s debauchery, or this morning’s. Stray dogs patrol the streets, trotting from one garbage pile to the next like derelict show ponies. In their glory days, they guarded the now-abandoned buildings that flank the street, too pure for this world with their barbed-wire crowns of thorns.

Baby birds are just waking up, warbling. They were promised a worm, like all early birds, but maybe they’ll settle for the gnats buzzing around my face, plentiful at these hours when it’s still not hot enough for the sun to burn them out of the air midflight.

It doesn’t take much to drown out the noise they make. Every half-minute, buses rattle up the sand-dusted Narciso Mendoza and down the Leona Vicario. As I turn onto Lázaro Cárdenas, I’m presented with a beautiful bouquet of belching tubas courtesy of the music blaring from the back of a black vocho. One doesn’t question who would blast banda music at this hour. “Reveille.” “La 4 x 4.” Same tiger, different stripes.

The soundtrack of the Cabo San Lucas Marina

The playlist in the Cabo San Lucas Marina is different. You might still hear some classics, depending on whose boat you walk by, but the shops and kiosks pander to a different demographic. I still haven’t quite figured out which. Daft Punk begets Murray Head, which begets Katy Perry. Speaking of which, Señor Frog’s is still thriving. Even at this hour, I spot a gringo retiree in board shorts and a tank top loitering in front, presumably curious about hours of operation. He’s in good company.

Along the esplanade, you hear far more English than Spanish. Much of that comes from merchants stumbling through back-of-the-napkin phrases they’ve committed to memory to entice newly arrived tourists to buy their wares. Though I also hear an old woman muttering something to her dog about one of the boats they pass by, so I guess even the dogs here are fluent.

‘A parking lot for yachts’

Along a wall, a line of men wearing Oakleys, long-sleeved shirts and visors sits idly, taking it easy before heading out on whatever excursions they’ll be leading. Nearby, a bored-looking clerk in a dockside store that looks like Cabo’s version of J. Peterman scrolls on his phone, unfazed about the urban sombrero sales quota he’ll need to meet by the end of the day. Even aboard the boats, on the eve of the world’s biggest marlin tournament, local fishermen prattle, hosing down decks and trying to be heard over the dull roar of idling boat engines.

This marina is like a Costco parking lot for yachts, though instead of an associate in a neon vest checking your ID, there’s a tall, wrought-iron gate with an entrance like a cage that only those with a key can get through. I pause to size it up, then look around to see who’s watching. “I could hop that,” I say to myself.

Ethan Jacobs is a freelance writer and writing coach based in Playa del Carmen. He has written extensively in narrative and short fiction formats, and his work has received recognition both domestically and internationally in microfiction, short fiction and narrative essay formats.

World.title: Is Chipotle in Mexico a good or bad idea? A ‘Confidently Wrong’ podcast
World.content:
Recently, and with much fanfare, Chipotle opened its first restaurant in Mexico. Perhaps not surprisingly, the opening spurred a polarizing debate and discussion about whether a U.S.-based Mexican restaurant chain would do well in the country. Years ago, Taco Bell entered the country and ultimately left in what was considered a disaster.

So what are the arguments for and against Chipotle coming to Mexico? Is it yet another unwanted assault of American culture on another country? Or is it a welcome sign of competition and choice for Mexicans?

Could it lead to lost business for local Mexican restaurants and reduced “authentic” Mexican food options? Or could it create a standard for the trifecta of affordability, service and quality that Chipotle is known for and oftentimes doesn’t exist in many restaurants today? Or perhaps it’s not that big of a deal, and people should move on?

And finally, what does the choice of a ritzy Monterrey suburb as the first restaurant location in the country tell us?

I will admit that while I have been a very frequent customer of Chipotle in the United States, I have actually eaten very few burritos here in Mexico. And the ones I have had have been very different.

In this week’s episode of Confidently Wrong, George and I talk through the arguments on each side of the debate and offer our own thoughts and opinions. Where do you stand on this issue? Check out the discussion here:

World.title: US sanctions more than 50 Jalisco cartel-linked individuals and businesses
World.content:
The U.S. Treasury on Thursday imposed sanctions on 39 Mexican individuals and 16 companies it alleges are linked to the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), calling it “the largest action ever taken” against the notorious crime gang.

The measure targets the leadership of the cartel — designated by President Donald Trump as a foreign terrorist organization — and its illicit financing networks across Mexico.

The Treasury Department said in a statement that the goal of the sanctions is to limit the CJNG’s ability to traffic fentanyl and other drugs into the United States.

Shortly thereafter, Mexico’s Financial Intelligence Unit (UIF) reported it had identified “indicators related to possible operations with resources of illicit origin, including cash transactions, acquisition of high-end vehicles, jewelry and real estate,” as well as “international transfers, intensive use of credit and debit cards and transactions using virtual assets.”

As a result of this review, Mexico blocked the accounts of the same 55 individuals and companies sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department.

“The coordinated actions between Mexican and U.S. authorities strengthen mechanisms of international cooperation to prevent abuse of the financial system, combat money laundering and weaken the economic structures of organized crime,” the UIF said.

Among those sanctioned is Juan Carlos González, aka “El Pelón,” identified by U.S. authorities as the new leader of the CJNG following the February death of his stepfather, cartel founder, Rubén Oseguera Cervantes, who was killed in a federal operation.

The U.S. State Department has offered a reward of US $5 million for the capture of González, who holds both Mexican and U.S. citizenship.

Also sanctioned was the network of associates and subordinates linked to Audias Flores Silva, aka El Jardinero, who was arrested by Mexican authorities in April.

The UIF review found “inconsistencies” in tax records involving the accused, saying “they present characteristics of shell companies or with corporate structures of limited or no apparent economic activity.”

A complaint was filed with the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) and the 39 individuals — as well as eight others accused of being part of the same CJNG network — were added to the UIF’s Blocked Persons List (BPL).

The BPL is a public report identifying individuals and legal entities involved in money laundering or terrorist financing. All Mexican individuals and companies are required to immediately suspend any and all acts, operations or services with people or entities on the BPL.

With reports from EFE, Infobae, El Economista and La Jornada

World.title: Hologram Zoo in Mexico City: Polar Bears, Dinosaurs from US$15
World.content:
LIFE: CIUDAD DE MÉXICO

Key Facts —Location. The Hologram Zoo sits in Plaza Carso, Miguel Hidalgo, across from Acuario Inbursa and Museo Soumaya. —Technology. It uses laser-based holograms, projections, sound, and special glasses to create life-size animals with no live exhibits. —Experiences. Visitors choose from Arctic, Africa, and Dinosaur zones, each a 45-minute guided walkthrough. —Pricing. Single experiences start at 299 pesos (roughly US$15). Combos for two zones cost around 540 pesos (US$27). —Accessibility. The venue is on one floor with ramps and no stairs, welcoming wheelchair users and all ages.

Mexico City has gained a new family attraction as the Hologram Zoo Mexico City opens in Plaza Carso, replacing live animals with laser-projected polar bears, dinosaurs, and African wildlife in an immersive walkthrough experience.

Mexico City has embraced immersive, screen-based attractions like the Hologram Zoo.

What the Hologram Zoo Mexico City Offers

The Hologram Zoo is an animal-themed attraction built entirely around digital projection technology. Visitors wear special glasses and walk through darkened tunnels and rooms where life-size creatures appear to move, breathe, and even approach them.

There are no live animals on site. The experience combines laser holograms, surround sound, and occasional scents to create the sensation of standing on an Arctic ice sheet or a Jurassic floodplain.

Three themed zones anchor the attraction. The Arctic zone features polar bears, emperor and macaroni penguins, orcas, and a giant holographic whale gliding overhead.

The Africa zone brings lions, leopards, elephants, rhinos, buffalo, giraffes, and hippos into savanna and jungle settings. The Dinosaur zone includes a brachiosaurus, triceratops, velociraptor, diplodocus, and a towering Tyrannosaurus rex in prehistoric landscapes.

Location and How to Get There

The Hologram Zoo sits in the Plaza Carso complex in the Miguel Hidalgo borough, one of the capital’s most visited cultural and commercial corridors. Its address is Ferrocarril de Cuernavaca s/n, Colonia Granada, directly across from the Acuario Inbursa aquarium.

Visitors can also find it at Bulevar Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra 380, colonia Irrigación, facing the Museo Soumaya. The two addresses refer to the same complex, which is well served by ride-hailing apps, the Metrobús, and nearby parking.

The area already draws heavy foot traffic for the aquarium, the Soumaya museum, and the upscale shopping and dining options inside Plaza Carso. Adding the Hologram Zoo strengthens the zone as a full-day destination for families and tourists.

Tickets, Pricing, and Schedule

A single experience costs 299 Mexican pesos per person, roughly US$15 at current exchange rates. Visitors who want to combine two zones can buy a combo ticket for around 540 pesos (US$27), with options such as Africa plus Dinosaurs or Arctic plus Dinosaurs.

The venue is open daily from 10:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. Each guided walkthrough lasts between 45 minutes and one hour, and groups enter at scheduled times with limited capacity.

Tickets are sold online through platforms such as Fever and at the venue itself. Advance purchase is recommended, especially on weekends and during school holidays, when slots fill quickly.

Who the Hologram Zoo Is For

The attraction is designed for all ages, from young children to adults. It targets families, school groups, tourists, and anyone interested in technology, wildlife, or educational entertainment without the ethical questions tied to traditional zoos.

The holographic format also appeals to visitors who want a climate-controlled, accessible outing. The entire venue operates on one floor with ramps and no stairs, making it navigable for wheelchair users and strollers.

The Business and Tourism Read-Through

Mexico City’s tourism sector continues to diversify beyond its historic centre and traditional museums. The Hologram Zoo represents a growing niche of tech-driven, indoor family attractions that can operate year-round regardless of weather or air quality.

For investors and expats, the Plaza Carso area remains one of Latin America’s most concentrated zones of cultural and commercial investment. The arrival of a new immersive attraction signals continued confidence in foot-traffic-driven retail and entertainment in Miguel Hidalgo.

The concept also taps into a global trend of animal-free immersive experiences, from Tokyo’s teamLab exhibitions to holographic zoos in Australia. Mexico City’s version brings that model to Latin America at an accessible price point, positioning it as both a local outing and a tourist draw.

What to Watch Next

Early visitor response and online booking patterns will indicate whether the Hologram Zoo can sustain daily operations beyond its opening buzz. The venue’s ability to refresh content with new animal zones or seasonal themes will likely determine repeat visitation.

Expats and long-term residents should watch for membership or multi-visit passes, which have not yet been announced but would align with the pricing model of similar attractions globally.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where is the Hologram Zoo in Mexico City located?

The Hologram Zoo is in Plaza Carso, Miguel Hidalgo, at Ferrocarril de Cuernavaca s/n, Colonia Granada. It sits directly across from Acuario Inbursa and next to Museo Soumaya, making it easy to combine with other attractions in the same complex.

How much do tickets cost for the Hologram Zoo Mexico City?

Single-zone tickets start at 299 pesos (about US$15) per person. Combo tickets covering two zones, such as Africa plus Dinosaurs or Arctic plus Dinosaurs, cost around 540 pesos (US$27).

Prices may vary by date and demand, and advance online booking is recommended.

Are there live animals at the Hologram Zoo?

No, the Hologram Zoo has no live animals. All creatures are life-size holograms and projections created with lasers, sound, and special glasses.

The experience is designed as an animal-free alternative to traditional zoos, suitable for all ages.

World.title: Chile’s Iconic Wetlands to Visit and Those Facing Extinction
World.content:
Environment & Travel

Key Facts —Total wetlands. Chile holds roughly 40,000 wetlands covering about 4.5 million hectares, or 6% of the national territory. —Protection gap. Only about 2% of mapped wetlands have any formal protection status, leaving the vast majority legally exposed. —Historical loss. An estimated 80% of Chilean wetlands have disappeared in the last 50 years due to urban growth, drainage, and agriculture. —Ramsar sites. Chile has 16 Ramsar Sites of international importance, covering roughly 363,927 hectares across the country. —Cartographic erasure. In a recent update, 539 wetlands were removed from Chile’s official biodiversity register, reducing the inventory from 2,461 to 1,922 ecosystems.

Chile’s wetlands span from high-altitude salt flats hosting three flamingo species to Patagonian peatlands that serve as critical carbon sinks, yet roughly 80% have been lost in half a century and over 40% of coastal sites now face high vulnerability.

Flamingos in the Atacama; Chile’s wetlands range from protected sanctuaries to habitats facing extinction.

The High-Andean Jewels of Chile’s Wetlands

The Salar de Surire in the Arica y Parinacota region sits at roughly 4,300 metres above sea level and hosts three of the world’s four flamingo species in a single location. Declared a Natural Monument and Ramsar Site, its white salt crusts and turquoise lagoons framed by snow-capped volcanoes make it one of the most photographed high-altitude landscapes in South America.

Further south, the Soncor Hydrological System inside the Salar de Atacama basin forms part of the Los Flamencos National Reserve and serves as the principal global breeding centre for the Andean flamingo. This same basin holds over 90% of Chile’s lithium reserves, placing it at the centre of a growing tension between conservation and the global energy transition.

The recently created Salar del Huasco National Park in the Tarapacá region protects another high-altitude salt flat where all three Chilean flamingo species coexist alongside vicuñas and alpacas. Its new park status signals a governmental push to safeguard these fragile ecosystems, though enforcement capacity remains limited.

Coastal Wetlands: Accessible and Under Siege

The El Yali wetland in the Valparaíso Region lies less than two hours from Santiago and hosts over 130 bird species, functioning as a critical stopover for migratory birds travelling between hemispheres. Its marked trails and visitor infrastructure make it one of the most accessible sites for travellers wanting to experience Chile’s wetlands firsthand.

Laguna Conchalí near Los Vilos in the Coquimbo Region remains one of the last intact coastal wetlands in the area, with more than 100 bird species recorded and a Nature Sanctuary designation dating back to 1996. The Batuco wetland, roughly 40 kilometres from Santiago, protects about 300 hectares and harbours 150-plus bird species including threatened ones like the reed cormorant.

A multi-scale vulnerability assessment found that 42.6% of evaluated coastal wetlands in Chile have high or very high vulnerability. The most exposed sites cluster in central Chile, where urban expansion, real-estate pressure, and reduced rainfall from climate change converge most intensely.

The Southern Riverine and Urban Wetland Networks

The Carlos Anwandter Nature Sanctuary on the Cruces River near Valdivia was Chile’s first Ramsar Site, designated in 1981, and remains the country’s most iconic riverine wetland. It is the principal habitat for the black-necked swan, an emblematic bird of southern Chile, and draws photographers and naturalists year-round.

The Rocuant-Andalién system in Concepción spans roughly 11 square miles and was designated a global Important Bird and Biodiversity Area by BirdLife International in 2021. Despite its international recognition, the complex has already been drastically reduced by industrial expansion and urban development, making it a emblematic case of an urban wetland system at risk.

Around Valdivia, the Angachilla and Llancahue wetlands form part of a network of Nature Sanctuaries that combine palustrine wetlands, flooded swamp forests, and remnants of ancient Valdivian temperate rainforest. Community-led conservation efforts in these peri-urban zones offer a model for balancing city growth with ecosystem protection.

Patagonian Peatlands and the Carbon Sink Factor

Patagonia’s vast peat bog complexes in the Aysén and Magallanes regions function as major carbon sinks, storing immense quantities of greenhouse gases in layers of partially decomposed vegetation. A new national law now explicitly recognises their role in climate mitigation, though poor extraction practices for “pompón” moss used in horticulture remain a serious threat.

Bahía Lomas in Tierra del Fuego is one of Chile’s most important coastal wetlands for migratory shorebirds, hosting large populations of Red Knot and other species that depend on its vast tidal flats. Its Ramsar designation underscores its hemispheric relevance, yet its extreme southern location means monitoring and enforcement are logistically challenging.

Chiloé Island alone concentrates roughly 29,500 hectares of wetlands embedded in a landscape of channels, estuaries, and peat bogs with strong cultural ties to local communities. The island’s wetland mosaic supports both traditional livelihoods and significant birdlife, including migratory shorebirds and waterfowl.

Lithium, Drought, and the Wetlands at Risk of Disappearing

The Salar de Atacama basin exemplifies the direct conflict between mineral extraction and wetland survival, with large-scale lithium operations drawing on the same groundwater that sustains flamingo breeding habitats. Regional analyses show that Andean wetlands across Chile, Argentina, and Bolivia face serious risk from expanding lithium and mineral extraction driven by global electric-vehicle demand.

Laguna Santa Rosa in the Atacama Region has already experienced documented environmental degradation and shrinking linked to mining and geothermal activities. The Limarí River wetland, designated a Ramsar Site in 2020, sits in a climate-change hotspot where severe drought and advancing desertification threaten to collapse its riverine ecosystem.

Arid coastal wetlands in northern Chile—including those at the mouths of the Lluta, Camarones, Loa, and Copiapó rivers—exist in zones of extreme water deficit and serve as crucial stopovers for migratory birds along the Pacific flyway. Many of these small sites go unnoticed in policy discussions despite facing threats from urbanisation, pollution, and water abstraction.

The Institutional Risk: When Wetlands Vanish from the Map

Civil society organisations recently reported that 539 wetlands were removed from Chile’s official biodiversity information system, shrinking the national register from 2,461 to 1,922 ecosystems. This cartographic erasure does not mean the wetlands have physically disappeared, but it strips them of legal recognition and leaves them more exposed to extractive or urban projects.

Only about 2% of Chile’s mapped wetlands have any formal protection status, whether as Ramsar sites, nature sanctuaries, or national park units. Restoration initiatives led by local communities and NGOs have recovered over 11,000 hectares across the country in recent years, demonstrating that degradation can be reversed when resources and political will align.

For investors and expats, the wetland protection gap represents both a regulatory risk and an emerging opportunity. Projects near vulnerable wetlands face growing scrutiny from communities and courts, while conservation finance and sustainable tourism ventures around iconic sites like El Yali or Carlos Anwandter are attracting increased attention.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which Chilean wetlands are easiest to visit from Santiago?

The Batuco wetland lies roughly 40 kilometres from the capital and hosts over 150 bird species with growing visitor infrastructure. El Yali in the Valparaíso Region is less than two hours away and offers marked trails, making it the most developed wetland tourism destination near Santiago.

Why are Chile’s high-altitude wetlands threatened by lithium mining?

The Salar de Atacama basin holds over 90% of Chile’s lithium reserves, and extraction operations pump brine from the same groundwater that sustains flamingo breeding habitats and high-Andean lagoons. Cumulative impacts on water balance threaten the entire hydrological system, with regional studies warning that Andean wetlands across Chile, Argentina, and Bolivia face serious risk from expanding mineral operations.

What does the removal of 539 wetlands from Chile’s official register mean?

The removal from the SIMBIO biodiversity information system does not indicate physical disappearance but rather a loss of official recognition in state maps. This cartographic erasure leaves affected wetlands legally unrecognised and more vulnerable to extractive or urban development projects, as they no longer appear in the inventories used for environmental impact assessments.

World.title: Cartagena’s Teatro Adolfo Mejía Opens 2026 Season with Classical Festival
World.content:
Culture & Heritage

Key Facts —Opening event. The 2026 season begins 4–12 January with the 20th Cartagena International Music Festival. —Scale. Twenty-seven concerts are programmed across the historic walled city, with Teatro Adolfo Mejía as the main night-time stage. —Theme. “El alma y el cuerpo: universalismo musical y escuelas nacionales” explores the tension between universal musical language and national schools. —Resident orchestra. The Franz Liszt Chamber Orchestra anchors the symphonic programme as the festival’s resident ensemble. —Year-round calendar. After January, the theatre hosts Hay Festival, FICCI film festival, jazz, theatre, and choral events through April and beyond.

The Teatro Adolfo Mejía 2026 cultural season formally opens in early January with the 20th edition of the Cartagena International Music Festival, reinforcing the venue’s role as the most important cultural stage in Colombia’s Caribbean and a draw for culturally minded investors and expats.

Cartagena’s historic Teatro Adolfo Mejía anchors the city’s 2026 cultural season.
