World.title: Washington rejects Iraq’s deal with Turkmenistan to import gas
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s plan to purchase Turkmen gas has encountered another obstacle, as the US has raised objections to Baghdad’s proposal to transport the supplies through Iranian territory.

A source told Attaqa News that the United States has connected the agreement’s execution to negotiating a comprehensive political solution with Tehran, complicating the issue of obtaining the fuel required to run Iraq’s power plants.

The US position emerged during talks held in Washington by a government delegation accompanying Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, which included Electricity Minister Ali Wahib and Oil Minister Basim Khudair.

The two sides discussed energy and economic cooperation, but the Turkmen gas sale to Iraq via Iran drew strong American opposition, despite Baghdad’s urgent need for new fuel sources amid a worsening electricity crisis.

The rejection comes amid escalating military operations in the Middle East, with the United States and Iran exchanging attacks, as well as rising tensions in the Arabian Gulf, which have affected maritime security in the Strait of Hormuz.

Iraq signed a memorandum of understanding in 2023 with Turkmenistan to import the necessary gas for its power plants, as stated by the Ministry of Electricity. The ministry indicated that the initiative will necessitate additional negotiations regarding the transportation of gas through Iran.

Power plants in Iraq depend on gas imports from Iran, which cover one-third of the country’s energy needs.

This agreement permits Iran to receive a quarter of the gas supplied across its borders.

The gas supply agreement with Turkmenistan aims to provide Iraq with an average of 20 million cubic meters per day.

World.title: Iraqi court seizes IQD 27 billion in Jumaili’s case
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s anti-corruption judiciary has seized IQD 27 billion in cash as part of an ongoing investigation involving Adnan Al-Jumaili, the detained former Deputy Oil Minister for Refining Affairs, in one of the country’s latest high-profile corruption cases.

Judicial authorities said the money was recovered during investigations into alleged financial losses linked to projects overseen by the former official and other individuals connected to the case.

In a statement issued on Sunday, the media office of Iraq’s judiciary said Judge Diaa Jaafar, the investigating judge at the Central Anti-Corruption Criminal Court, confirmed the seizure of IQD 27 billion.

According to the court, the funds were discovered after investigators traced financial proceeds allegedly generated through waste and irregularities in projects associated with Al-Jumaili and other suspects.

Officials said the cash had been hidden by several individuals believed to be involved in the case. The court said investigators are continuing to pursue additional suspects and trace other assets that may be linked to the alleged offenses.

Judicial authorities indicated that the investigation remains active as efforts continue to identify everyone involved and recover additional public funds, if any are found.

The judiciary also released photographs showing stacks of newly recovered banknotes arranged in large piles following the seizure. According to the statement, the images document the IQD 27 billion recovered during Sunday’s operation, which authorities said had been concealed by individuals connected to the former deputy minister.

Officials did not disclose how many people are under investigation or provide further details about the locations where the money was found.

The case is among several recent corruption investigations pursued by Iraq’s anti-corruption courts as authorities seek to recover public funds and hold officials accountable for alleged financial crimes.

The judiciary reiterated that investigations remain ongoing and that further legal action could follow as additional evidence emerges.

World.title: Iraq completes initial designs for Development Road Project
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq has completed the preliminary designs for its flagship Development Road Project and railway corridor, marking a major milestone as the government prepares to advance one of its largest infrastructure initiatives into the implementation phase.

The Ministry of Transport announced on Sunday that the initial designs are now 100% complete, with work shifting to detailed engineering plans covering infrastructure, bridges, railway stations, and technical facilities along the project’s route.

According to a source at the ministry’s media office, engineers have begun preparing the project’s detailed designs to ensure the corridor meets international engineering and construction standards. The next phase includes finalizing plans for the railway network, highways, bridges, stations, and supporting infrastructure before construction begins.

Officials described the transition as a key step toward launching the long-awaited project after completing the necessary preparatory stages.

The announcement follows a recent visit by Turkish Transport Minister Abdulkadir Uraloğlu to Baghdad on July 21, where he held talks with Iraqi officials on strengthening cooperation in transport and communications.

During the meetings, Iraqi Transport Minister Wahb Al-Hassani and his Turkish counterpart agreed to accelerate technical planning and implementation procedures for the Development Road Project.

The ministry said both sides consider the corridor a transformative initiative that could reshape regional trade and economic cooperation. The ministry also revealed that Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi has instructed officials to prepare a comprehensive financing mechanism for the project.

Securing funding will be a priority ahead of the project’s implementation and is expected to feature prominently during Al-Zaidi’s upcoming visit to Ankara, where discussions with Turkish officials will focus on advancing strategic cooperation and moving the project toward construction.

The Development Road Project is designed to create a major transport corridor linking Iraq’s ports with regional and international markets. The combined railway and highway network aims to connect the Grand Faw Port in southern Iraq with Turkey and Europe, positioning Iraq as a key logistics hub between Asia and Europe.

Officials say the corridor will significantly improve trade flows while strengthening Iraq’s role in global supply chains. Alongside the engineering work, the Ministry of Transport is preparing the project’s economic model to maximize investment returns and attract local and international partners.

The ministry said the framework will also align with the government’s broader reform agenda, including digital transformation and modern project management systems.

The government views the Development Road Project as one of Iraq’s most important strategic investments. Officials expect it to diversify the economy beyond oil, generate new non-oil revenues, attract foreign investment, and create thousands of jobs across multiple sectors.

By leveraging Iraq’s geographic position between East and West, the project is also expected to strengthen the country’s role as a regional center for transportation, logistics, and international trade.

World.title: Iraq’s non-oil revenues jump to 16%
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Eco Iraq Observatory, which studies economic performance indicators, disclosed on Saturday that non-oil income now accounts for 16 percent of Iraq’s overall financial revenues, the highest percentage recorded so far.

According to a statement released by the observatory, this is the first time that the percentage of non-oil earnings has climbed to 16 percent during the months of May and June, having not exceeded five percent in years.

Eco Iraq noted that the proportion originally grew to roughly 10 percent between May 2020 and October 2022, then remained stable at that level during Mohammed Shia Al-Sudani’s leadership before recently hitting its peak.

The statement highlighted that non-oil revenues are divided into commodity taxes, production fees, general fees, income and wealth taxes, transfer revenues, and other sources.

Iraqi Kurdistan’s income, which it distributes to the federal government in Baghdad, accounts for around 5.5 percent of overall non-oil revenues.

As part of the government’s efforts to diversify the economy and achieve Iraq’s long-term development goals, Mazhar Saleh, the Prime Minister’s Advisor for Financial Affairs, stated in early June that an initiative would be launched. This initiative aims to create an integrated link between enhancing the structure of non-oil revenues within the framework of state finances and diversifying the non-oil GDP.

The Iraqi government established the ambitious goal, referred to as ‘Iraq 2035,’ in May. It includes both public finance reforms and social market economy policies, which aim to facilitate a gradual structural transformation of the national economy, as stated by Saleh.

The vision transforms fiscal policy to ensure that non-oil income accounts for at least 46 percent of total governmental revenues. This will improve budgetary sustainability and reduce the volatility caused by overreliance on oil earnings.

World.title: Iraq to launch ferry routes to Iran, Kuwait, UAE, and Saudi Arabia
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq is preparing to launch a network of regular maritime passenger routes connecting the country with Iran, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, and Saudi Arabia, as part of a broader effort to revive the country’s maritime transport sector and strengthen regional tourism.

According to Iraq’s Ministry of Transport, the initiative will begin after technical and administrative requirements are completed in coordination with relevant authorities inside Iraq and neighboring countries.

A source at the ministry’s media office told Iraq’s official newspaper that the government has developed a comprehensive plan to operate regional maritime transport services using an expanded fleet of boats and ferries.

The ministry currently operates 40 boats and ferries under its river transport program and has recently added 15 new boats and three ferries to the fleet. The upgraded vessels are expected to provide modern, safe transportation for passengers while supporting Iraq’s growing tourism sector.

According to the ministry, most of the new vessels will be deployed on passenger and tourism routes linking Iraq with Kuwait, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Iran. Officials said services will begin once all operational approvals, safety procedures, and cross-border coordination have been finalized to ensure the routes meet international maritime safety standards.

The planned connections are expected to facilitate both tourism and commercial travel between Iraq and neighboring countries. The Ministry of Transport believes the new maritime routes will provide an affordable and practical alternative for regional travel, particularly for leisure tourism.

The project is also expected to improve mobility for official delegations and religious visitors while strengthening economic ties with Gulf states and Iran through enhanced passenger connectivity.

Officials described the initiative as a significant step toward revitalizing Iraq’s maritime transport sector after years of limited regional ferry services. The ferry project forms part of a wider government strategy to modernize Iraq’s river and maritime transport infrastructure.

Alongside expanding its fleet, the ministry is investing in the development of ports, docks, and river terminals to improve passenger services and operational efficiency.

The broader vision aims to restore river and maritime transport as an important component of Iraq’s transportation network while supporting economic development, tourism, and greater regional integration.

World.title: Kirkuk Engineers Syndicate accuses BP of sidelining local talent and demands an 85% local hiring quota
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Kirkuk Engineers Syndicate has voiced strong concerns over hiring practices and subcontract awards linked to BP’s operations in the province’s oil fields, alleging that local engineers and businesses are being overlooked in favor of workers and companies from outside Kirkuk.

While welcoming international investment in Iraq’s energy sector, the syndicate warned it would pursue legal action and peaceful protests if local employment requirements are not enforced.

In a statement, the syndicate said it is closely monitoring recruitment procedures and the awarding of secondary contracts related to BP’s projects in Kirkuk.

It argued that the current approach has resulted in several violations, including the exclusion of qualified local engineers despite the availability of experienced graduates and professionals from the province.

The syndicate also claimed that engineering and technical staff are being recruited from outside Kirkuk, while numerous subcontracting and logistics contracts have been awarded to companies based elsewhere.

According to the statement, these practices undermine the local economy and deprive Kirkuk residents of employment opportunities linked to projects operating within their province.

The syndicate stressed that Kirkuk residents bear the environmental and health impacts associated with oil production and should therefore receive priority in employment opportunities.

It called on the Ministry of Oil and the Kirkuk provincial administration to require that at least 85% of jobs across all project stages be reserved exclusively for residents of Kirkuk.

In addition, the syndicate demanded formal representation on the joint recruitment committee to ensure transparency and fairness in hiring decisions. It also urged authorities to use the syndicate’s database of registered engineering graduates when filling vacancies.

Among its proposals, the syndicate called for all job applications to be processed exclusively through the employment office of the Kirkuk Governorate, arguing that a centralized system would improve transparency and ensure equal access to opportunities.

The organization also backed government efforts to distribute employment opportunities fairly among all communities in Kirkuk without discrimination.

The statement concluded with a warning that the syndicate would not remain silent if local engineers continue to be excluded from employment opportunities.

It said it is prepared to coordinate with legislative and executive authorities and pursue all available legal avenues, alongside peaceful protests, to protect the rights of Kirkuk’s engineering community. The statement did not include a response from BP regarding the allegations.

World.title: Iraq’s central bank improves non-bank financial oversight
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – As part of a major institutional reform, the Central Bank of Iraq (CBI) upgraded its Directorate of Non-Bank Financial Institutions Supervision to a complete General Directorate.

This change intends to increase regulatory control, develop digital solutions, and improve institutional performance in Iraq’s expanding financial industry.

The reform entails significant changes to departments, name practices, and reporting structures.

The newly established general directorate will include all important departments in charge of policy, regulatory structures, digital technologies, and financial service operations.

The Information Technology and Payments Directorate is now known simply as the Information Technology Directorate. Its old financial inclusion and information security sections have been removed and merged with risk management and other operational directorates.

The CBI closed its office for coordinating branch activities. The major branches in Basra, Mosul, and Erbil will report directly to the bank’s deputy governor.

The Human Resources Directorate has directed that all personnel transfers and systemic transitions will be effective by July 30, 2026.

This change corresponds with CBI Governor Nizar Hussein’s increasing regulatory push on financial technology businesses to decrease cash dependency and adhere to international compliance requirements.

World.title: Iran destroys nearly all US military facilities in Iraq’s Erbil
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iranian army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia said that the IRGC destroyed nearly all US military installations during recent operations in Erbil, the capital of the Kurdistan region of Iraq.

Akraminia stated Tehran was now using newer attack drones that were more accurate and sophisticated than the Arash-2, according to Anadolu Agency (AA).

The Iranian official claimed that Iran has severely damaged US military outposts around the region, with many losing most of their operational capabilities.

Akraminia also indicated that Iran is prepared to persist with military operations until the United States acknowledges its inability to impose its will on the nation through violent means.

Akraminia claimed that anti-Iranian Kurdish resistance groups based in Erbil are also no longer able to carry out missions because of the destroyed infrastructure.

Reports mentioned that, while the bases have suffered damage, allegations of complete destruction are greatly overstated.

World.title: 'Govt-ordered probe an eyewash': Tripura Congress MLA demands judicial inquiry into DGP Anurag Dhankar's death
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Tripura Congress MLA Sudip Roy Barman on Sunday reiterated the party's demand for a judicial probe into the death of state DGP Anurag Dhankar, who was found dead at the police headquarters in Agartala on July 20.

"From day one, we have been demanding a judicial probe by a sitting high court judge into the unnatural death of the DGP, keeping in mind the circumstances leading to the recovery of his body," he told a press conference at the Congress Bhavan in Agartala.

"The condition in which we saw his body at the morgue was as if he was in deep sleep, with no visible wounds that are generally found in such cases. We strongly believe that a team led by an SP-rank officer cannot clear the many doubts surrounding the incident.

That is why we want a judicial inquiry into the unnatural death," Roy Barman added.

A three-member team headed by West Tripura SP Namit Pathak has been constituted to investigate the matter.

Roy Barman termed the Tripura government's decision to investigate the case through a three-member team as an "eyewash." He alleged that the "honest DGP was heckled over some issues days before his death."

The Congress MLA also expressed disappointment over the Tripura high court not taking suo motu cognisance of Dhankar's death.





"The people of the state are also upset over the role of our high court. When the legislature, bureaucracy and media succumb, it is the judiciary that comes out and stands for the cause of people's rights. Unfortunately, we have not seen the high court take any suo motu cognisance in many incidents in the state since former Chief Justice Deepak Kumar Gupta's tenure ended," he said.

Dhankar, a native of Uttar Pradesh's Baghpat, was a 1994-batch IPS officer of the Tripura cadre. He took over as the state's DGP in May 2025.

The officer had led the CBI probe into the alleged Rs 13,000-crore Punjab National Bank fraud involving diamantaire Nirav Modi and the reinvestigation into the 1984 anti-Sikh riots.

(With PTI inputs)

World.title: From Chita Andolan to Jal Satyagrahas: Why the Ken-Betwa project has upset MP tribals
World.content:
NEW DELHI: They first stood in the river. Then they lay beside funeral pyres. When that, too, failed to draw a response, they climbed symbolic gallows.

Over the past month, the 'Chita Andolan' in Madhya Pradesh has transformed an otherwise local land acquisition dispute into one of the country's most striking protest movements, that was forcefully ended by the administration, citing threats to protesters due to rising water levels.

Its haunting imagery, however, has thrown a spotlight on the repercussions that the Ken-Betwa River Linking Project, a flagship infrastructure initiative that promises water security for millions but has also triggered a fierce battle over compensation, will have on the locals, questioning the rehabilitation and the rights of tribal communities facing displacement.

The movement gathered further attention after activist Amit Bhatnagar completed an 18-day hunger strike, insisting he had only suspendedânot endedâhis fast because "until the last person gets justice, the fast will continue."

Bhatnagar broke the hunger strike because villagers, especially women and children and 400 leading social activists from across the country, including

appealed to him since his health had started deteriorating. But it was the government's assurance of a fresh survey to include the names of those left out from rehabilitation that changed his decision.

Bhatnagar's protest became the face of growing resistance to the 'Ken-Betwa River Linking Project', India's first river-linking initiative under the National Perspective Plan.





The Centre and the Madhya Pradesh government hail the project as a landmark intervention that will transform the drought-prone Bundelkhand region through irrigation, drinking water supply and power generation. But for thousands of tribal families living in its path, it has become a battle over land, forests, livelihoods and identity.

Over the past month, villagers have staged some of the country's most striking demonstrations.

They stood waist-deep in river water in 'Jal Satyagraha', lay beside symbolic funeral pyres in the 'Chita Andolan' and even climbed symbolic gallows in a 'Faansi Satyagraha'.

Police eventually cleared the protest site on July 19, citing safety concerns due to rising water levels in the Barana river. Protesters alleged they were forcibly removed, while the administration maintained that the evacuation was necessary to prevent loss of life.

The movement has revived questions India has wrestled with since the Narmada Bachao Andolan: Can large infrastructure projects be built without sacrificing the rights of the communities that bear their greatest costs?

TIMELINE | Ken-Betwa Project

A project decades in the making



The Ken-Betwa Link Project has its origins in the National Perspective Plan for interlinking rivers proposed in 1980. After decades of planning, agreements and environmental clearances, the Union Cabinet approved the project in 2021, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi laid its foundation stone in December 2024.

The project proposed to transfer what the government describes as surplus water from the Ken river to the Betwa river through the Daudhan Dam, tunnels and a 221-kilometre canal.

The project is expected to irrigate 10.61 lakh hectares, providing drinking water to around 65 lakh people in Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh, generating 103 MW of hydropower and 27 MW of solar power and reduce the chronic water scarcity that has plagued Bundelkhand for decades.

Officials argue that it will boost agricultural productivity, reduce migration and improve groundwater recharge by restoring historical Chandela-era ponds.

For supporters, however, it is a long-awaited solution to one of central India's most persistent development challenges.

The surplus water of Ken River will be transferred to Betwa River through the 221 km long link canal from Daudhan Dam, providing irrigation and drinking water facilities in both MP and UP.

Why are people protesting?

For many tribal families in Chhatarpur and Panna districts, the project threatens the loss of ancestral land without adequate rehabilitation.

Bhatnagar says the issue extends far beyond compensation. "Our demand is that people should be given land in exchange for land. But even if the government only fulfils what it has committed, that much should at least be delivered."

He argues that tribal communities who depend on forests cannot rebuild their lives simply through financial assistance. "People who are being displaced from forests should either be resettled in forest areas or, at the very least, they should be given land and a village to live in.

That has been our main demand from the beginning."

The state government had announced an in-principle increase in the rehabilitation package from Rs 5 lakh to Rs 12.5 lakh per eligible displaced family, with a formal notification expected.

Bhatnagar, however, says the revised compensation alone does not solve the problem. "The way these people lived in forests and depended on the forest, simply giving them Rs 12.5 lakh is not enough."

He claims many displaced villagers have little experience navigating land markets and are vulnerable to exploitation. "Unscrupulous people are misleading them by offering fake land at cheap prices. They end up buying fake land or fake houses. Later they discover that the property itself was fraudulent. They lose both their money and then get trapped in legal disputes."

TIMELINE | CHITA ANDOLAN

One of the biggest disagreements concerns the number of affected families.

The government estimates that around 7,100 families are affected by the Ken-Betwa project. Bhatnagar disputes that figure.

"In the Ken-Betwa project, the government says there are 7,100 affected families. But the actual number is around 10,000, in fact more than 10,000. If we talk about all the projects together, nearly 50,000 people have been affected."

He alleges that survey teams have excluded genuine beneficiaries.

"The survey teams have included the names of many fake beneficiaries. For example, in one village where Rs 11 crore was sanctioned for housing compensation, Rs 8 crore went to fake beneficiaries, while only Rs 3 crore reached the actual villagers."

While the administration has rejected allegations of corruption, a fresh survey team was announced to identify families who may have been left out.

TOI reached out to Chhatarpur district magistrate and is still awaiting a response from the administration.

We will update the story accordingly.

The govt's fresh assurances made Bhatnagar suspend his hunger strike. "The administration did whatever it could from its side. It formed a new survey team for those people who had been left out. Our farmers' organisation has also been included in that survey team so that the names of everyone who was left out can be properly verified."

"We remain hopeful. But the officers and employees working for the government function very slowly.

Their pens don't move unless money is involved. We have faith in the government. But if the government does not do this, then our protest will continue," he warned, despite being hopeful.

The unique protest has drawn national attention.

How the 'Chita Andolan' was born

Perhaps the most striking aspect of the movement has been its symbolism.

The image of tribal families lying beside funeral pyres captured national attention and prompted comparisons with the Narmada Bachao Andolan's iconic Jal Satyagrahas.

Bhatnagar says the idea emerged after protesters felt every avenue of democratic dissent had been blocked. "Wherever we tried to protest, Section 144 notices were imposed. People were intimidated. When we were trying to go to Delhi, we were stopped, our vehicles fined, our entire stock of rations looted. We were stopped at several places."

He alleges that even after the movement got restricted to the villages, essential supplies were cut off.

"Food and water were cut off. Water tankers were removed. Even the borewell that was supplying water was shut down. We were forced to drink river water."

Then came the thought that gave the protest its name.

"If they are trying to kill us anyway, if our own government wants us to die, then let us light our own funeral pyre," said Bhatnagar.

As restrictions tightened, the forms of protest evolved.

"There were other forms of protest too, like standing in the river.

Then the Jal Satyagraha began. After that, they stopped our ration, food, medicines and even doctors from reaching us. Then they threatened us, saying they would hang us. So we ourselves climbed onto the gallows. That is how one form of protest after another kept evolving."

Why was the protest site cleared

The protest took another turn on July 19, when police dispersed demonstrators. Officials said continuous rainfall had raised the river level, making the site unsafe, and shifted Bhatnagar to hospital after his health deteriorated.

Bhatnagar alleges that women were injured during the operation. "Women's sarees were torn, many women lost their mangalsutras, and many people were injured. Naturally, there is a lot of anger among the people," he said.

Despite the anger, he insists the movement remains committed to non-violence.

"We follow Gandhian principles and believe in democratic values. We do not want such things. Yes, there is tremendous anger.

There is pain. Our effort is to maintain a balance between that pain and anger, and to ensure that people get justice through the right path," he said.

More than one project

While public attention has focused on the Ken-Betwa link, Bhatnagar says the movement also represents people affected by the Majhgaon and Runjh irrigation projects.

"There are five such projects in Chhatarpur and Panna where the law has not been followed."

He says surveys have restarted only in a limited area. "Right now, this process has begun only in a small area, in 11 villages of the Chhatarpur project.

The people of Panna district have not yet received any response."

The larger debate



The Ken-Betwa project has also faced criticism from environmental groups concerned about the impact of the Daudhan Dam on parts of the Panna Tiger Reserve. Conservationists have questioned forest submergence and biodiversity loss, while the government says all necessary environmental clearances have been obtained and mitigation measures are in place.

Ultimately, the dispute has become larger than one dam or one canal.

It reflects a recurring question in India's development journey: Can projects that promise benefits for millions be implemented without leaving displaced communities behind?

For the government, the Ken-Betwa project is a blueprint for India's future water security.

For many tribal families living along the Barana river, it is a fight to ensure that development does not come at the cost of their homes, livelihoods and identity.

As survey teams begin their work once again, the project's success may ultimately depend not only on engineering but on whether the promises of rehabilitation and justice reach every family that stands to lose the most.

World.title: ‘No law bars eating chicken over Ganga’: SC judge flags delayed bail at NLIU lecture
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan on Saturday questioned the criminalisation of ordinary activities while highlighting delays in granting relief to citizens facing criminal action for protest or dissent, saying there is "no law prohibiting consumption of chicken over the Ganga river.

"

Speaking at the Justice GP Singh 4th Memorial Lecture at the National Law Institute University (NLIU) in Bhopal, Justice Bhuyan cited the arrest of 14 Muslim men who were accused of consuming chicken biryani while breaking their Ramzan fast on a boat in the Ganga as an example of what he described as the criminalisation of normal activities.

"Take for example the case of a group of youngsters breaking their fast over the river Ganga by consuming chicken biryani. I am sure consuming chicken biryani is not an offence. It can't be an offence. There is no law prohibiting consumption of chicken over the Ganga river. They were arrested for that very reason and they had to remain in jail for 3 months," he said, as quoted by

Bar and Bench

.

Justice Bhuyan said such cases also highlighted broader concerns over how courts deal with petitions filed by citizens accused in protest-related cases.

He observed that while courts often grant bail or other relief, it frequently comes after considerable delay and is accompanied by restrictive conditions.

Raises concerns over delayed bail, restrictive conditions

The judge said the space for expressing divergent opinions in India was shrinking and cautioned against the criminalisation of peaceful democratic activities.





"It will not be an exaggeration to say that public space for expressing divergent opinion is shrinking in India. The right to express one's views and to demonstrate peacefully are fundamental freedoms of the citizens. Debate and dissent are the essence of democracy. Unfortunately, even normal activities are being criminalised," he said.

Justice Bhuyan also questioned the nature of conditions imposed while granting bail, suggesting that some restrictions could have a chilling effect on citizens exercising their right to dissent.

"These issues raise serious questions. Citizens are finding that though the courts are responsive and do grant bail, do grant relief, many a times it is belated. But it is the restrictive conditions which are imposed while granting bail that are causing the greatest concern. By such restrictive orders, are the courts indirectly telling the citizens or discouraging the citizens not to express their dissent?" he said.

He also cited cases where courts granted bail but directed accused persons not to attend public meetings, post on social media or leave the country, saying such conditions could undermine fundamental freedoms.

Refers to Bombay HC order on Gaza protest

Justice Bhuyan also referred to a July 2025 Bombay high court order dismissing a petition filed by the Communist Party of India (Marxist), which had sought permission to hold a protest at Mumbai's Azad Maidan against the alleged genocide in Gaza.

The high court had observed, "Our country has enough issues. We don't want anything like this. I am sorry to say, you are all short-sighted. You are looking at issues in Gaza and Palestine. Look at your own country. Be patriots. This is not patriotism. People say they are patriots."

Commenting on the order, Justice Bhuyan said he found it "very amusing" that a judge questioned why citizens wished to protest over developments outside India.

Calls for scrutiny of judicial decisions

Justice Bhuyan said the judiciary is not above criticism and stressed that judgments should be critically examined by lawyers, students and the wider legal community.

"Judgments, after being delivered, are required to be critically examined and criticised if necessary. Criticism of a judgment does not amount to criticism of a judge."

Referring to recent Supreme Court decisions, including the verdict on reservation for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS), he encouraged students to analyse judgments critically rather than accepting them unquestioningly.

"If everybody goes and tells the judges, 'Sir, wonderful thing. Sir, what you say is excellent. Sir, you are a jurist,' then how will the system improve?" he said.

Justice Bhuyan also said judges should regularly introspect if they wish to retain public confidence in the institution.

"For the judges and the judiciary to remain legitimate and to remain relevant, public perception is most crucial... It is not for us to make that comment.

It is for the citizens to assess. Perception of the citizens as to where the judiciary stands today, more particularly the Supreme Court, 75 years after we have become a Republic, is what matters," he said.

He added that institutional improvement depends on introspection and that robust public debate, including criticism of judicial decisions, strengthens democratic institutions.

Similar concerns raised earlier

Justice Bhuyan has previously voiced similar concerns about shrinking space for debate and dissent.

Speaking at a Supreme Court Bar Association conference in Bengaluru earlier this year, he said a developed India would require greater tolerance for diverse views and cautioned against criminalising dissent.

During that address, he also questioned the extensive use of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), pointing to low conviction rates and arguing that prolonged incarceration without timely trials could not be a model for a developed nation.

World.title: Beyond Tigers: The wildlife trade fuelled by pets and myths
World.content:
Binturong

Coolie

From forest animal to social-media prop

Egyptian vulture

When beauty and belief become threats

A crisis hiding in plain sight

The bazaar and the smartphone

Shikra

Looking beyond the flagship species

Dr. Ridhima Solanki holds a PhD in Natural Resources and Wildlife Sciences and a Master's in Forestry, with over a decade of experience shaping wildlife policy and practice across India and Southeast Asia.

Somewhere in the collective memory of Indian cinema perches Allah Rakha, the trained bird of prey fromthat generations of filmgoers grew up watching. It was a small but glamorous detail in a blockbuster, a wild creature transformed into a loyal companion. It would be difficult to prove that any one film encouraged the wildlife trade. Yet such portrayals can make proximity to a wild animal appear exciting, harmless and even aspirational. The reality behind that image is far less charming.A 2020 study of Facebook groups and pages in Thailand recorded 396 raptors and owls offered for sale between February 2015 and June 2019. These included nine shikras. Researchers found evidence that wild birds, including chicks taken from nests, were being offered online; one juvenile shikra was explicitly advertised as wild-caught.The falcon story, then, is not an isolated cultural memory. It points to a trade that has moved from cages in traditional markets to photographs, private messages and social-media listings.Earlier this month, a joint operation by the Central Bureau of Investigation and the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence, supported by the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau, recovered 53 protected animals and birds from locations in Maharashtra and West Bengal.The haul included 15 slow lorises, two binturongs, 28 star tortoises, six Egyptian vultures and two shikras. Six people were arrested in connection with what investigators described as an alleged interstate wildlife-trafficking syndicate. The investigation remains under way. The raid was an important enforcement success. It was also a window into a conservation crisis that rarely receives the attention reserved for tiger skins, elephant ivory or rhino horn.Slow lorises are especially vulnerable to the visual economy of the exotic-pet trade. Their large eyes and seemingly gentle movements make them attractive subjects for videos, tourist photographs and online posts. What looks endearing on a screen can conceal capture, transport, injury and prolonged stress.Studies of the tourist-photo trade have documented nocturnal slow lorises being exposed to bright lights and repeated flash photography, conditions that can disrupt their natural activity patterns and potentially damage their light-sensitive eyes.The physical toll can be severe. Researchers examining 77 confiscated greater slow lorises taken to a rehabilitation centre in Indonesia found that 28.6% died within six months, mostly because of traumatic injuries. All the infants in the group died. External wounds, dental problems and abnormal behaviour were common among those that survived. The study did not claim that every injury occurred during capture or transport, but it demonstrated the extraordinary welfare cost carried by animals moving through the illegal trade.By the time a wild animal appears in someoneâs home or on a touristâs shoulder, others may already have died along the supply chain. The binturong faces a similar pressure. A 2024 study of online trade in Indonesia found 594 s offering 724 live binturongs, with 97.6% of the listings appearing on Facebook. Researchers concluded that the exotic-pet trade appeared to be the principal source of demand in their dataset. Although the exact origins of most animals could not be established, the authors argued that a large share were probably taken illegally from the wild. Seizure records from 2015 to 2023 included 103 live binturongs. The evidence comes from Indonesia, and should not automatically be treated as a measure of the trade in India. But it shows how quickly demand for a relatively little-known forest animal can grow once buyers and sellers find one another online.Not every trafficked animal is bought for the same reason. The Indian star tortoise is prized for the striking pattern on its shell and is widely sought in the exotic-pet trade. In some markets, demand is also reinforced by beliefs that tortoises bring luck, prosperity or blessings. Those beliefs may sound benign, but they can turn a wild animal into an object of possession and encourage the removal of thousands of individuals from their natural habitat.The Egyptian vultures recovered during the CBI-DRI operation require more careful interpretation. The official release confirms their recovery but does not say why they were being traded or what the intended buyers planned to do with them. It would therefore be premature to attribute this particular seizure to occult practices, medicine or any other specific purpose. What is clear is that the Egyptian vulture is already endangered and faces several established threats, including poisoning, unsafe veterinary drugs, electrocution and the ingestion of contaminated carcasses. Illegal capture or trade adds another hazard to a species that has little room left for additional pressure.The larger lesson is that wildlife trafficking is not one market. It is a collection of overlapping markets driven by pets, status, food, traditional practices, decorative value and beliefs about luck or healing. Different species enter the chain for different reasons, but the result is often the same, an animal is removed from the wild and reduced to a commodity.Public attention to wildlife crime naturally gravitates towards tigers, elephants and rhinos. Sustained focus on these species has helped strengthen legislation, enforcement and public awareness. But the success of flagship-species conservation can create a blind spot. It can leave the impression that the broader war on wildlife trafficking is being won, even as birds, reptiles, primates and small carnivores continue to move through less visible networks.A Lok Sabha reply issued in August 2025 listed 820 wildlife-crime cases reported to the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau in 2020, followed by 632 in 2021, 546 in 2022, 349 in 2023 and 354 in 2024. These were cases registered and reported by state and central enforcement agencies. They are not estimates of the total number of wildlife crimes committed.The numbers therefore require care. The broad decline may indicate better deterrence, changing enforcement priorities or variations in reporting. It may also reflect the growing difficulty of detecting transactions that have moved online. The small increase from 349 cases in 2023 to 354 in 2024 also means the series is not an uninterrupted annual fall. A detected case tells us that enforcement found something. A falling number of detected cases does not, by itself, tell us whether the underlying trade is shrinking.The modern wildlife trade does not require the dark web. Ordinary social-media platforms are sufficient. A photograph can function as a shop window. The price can be negotiated through a private message. Buyers and sellers may never meet until the animal is delivered or handed to an intermediary. Research on the online trade in raptors and binturongs shows how public or semi-private social-media groups can connect sellers with a large customer base while making monitoring difficult.But the smartphone has not replaced the traditional wildlife market. The two systems can coexist. Repeated enforcement operations at Delhiâs Kabutar Market near Jama Masjid illustrate the resilience of the physical trade. Wildlife SOS reported that 1,741 birds, including around 500 chicks, were recovered in a 2022 operation. In July 2024, the Delhi Forest Department recovered around 1,000 birds following a complaint by PETA India. Nearly 150 more parakeets and pigeons were recovered in another operation that December.These figures do not establish that every trader in the market is involved in illegal activity. They do, however, show that protected native birds have repeatedly been found within an established commercial space. An IndiaSpend investigation into bird markets in Delhi, Patna and Lucknow also reported sales of protected species, poor welfare conditions and widespread non-compliance with registration requirements. Such findings should be attributed to the specific investigation rather than used to condemn every pet-shop owner or vendor in those cities.Under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (Pet Shop) Rules, establishments selling live animals are required to register and maintain prescribed welfare and record-keeping standards. Separately, the Wild Life (Protection) Act regulates the possession and trade of protected wildlife. Registration as a pet shop does not authorise a business to sell a protected native species.Raids matter. They rescue individual animals, disrupt supply chains and create consequences for traffickers. But repeated recoveries from the same markets show the limits of enforcement that addresses supply without reducing demand. Protecting biodiversity will require closer monitoring of online platforms, better coordination among forest departments, police, customs authorities and courier networks, and consistent action against the illegal sale of protected species. Social-media companies must also become more effective at identifying and removing wildlife-sale posts rather than relying largely on outside researchers and activists to flag them.Public behaviour matters just as much. A person posing with a nocturnal primate may see only an unusual holiday photograph. A buyer taking home a tortoise may believe that one small purchase cannot harm a species. Someone sharing an exotic-pet video may not know whether the animal was legally bred or pulled from the wild.But demand is built from individual acts. Every impulsive purchase, paid photograph and viral post can add value to the next animal waiting to be captured. South Asiaâs conservation story cannot end with the tiger, the elephant or the rhino. Its future also depends on the shikra in the cage, the loris under the camera flash, the tortoise hidden inside a bag and the binturong advertised through a phone screen. These are the creatures that rarely command front pages. They are also the ones the wildlife trade is counting on nobody to notice.

World.title: 'Misrepresents statement': MEA fact-checks viral claim on spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal's remarks on CJP protests
World.content:
MEA Spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe the claims of foreign funding behind the CJP protests are justified? Yes, there is a basis for these claims No, the claims are unfounded 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) on Sunday termed as "misleading" a social media post claiming that ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal had said there was no foreign funding behind the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led youth protest in Delhi.The CJP stir, followed by demonstrations in other parts of the country, led to the resignation of Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the alleged NEET (UG) question paper leak and other related issues."The post is misleading and misrepresents the statement of the spokesperson," the MEA's fact-check unit wrote on X, referring to the statement attributed to Jaiswal.It also shared Jaiswal's actual response to a query on allegations of foreign funding behind the CJP-led demonstrations."Madhu, regarding the point you raised about allegations of foreign funding and other such claims in connection with the ongoing protests, I would like to say that I do not have any information on this matter to share with you at this time," he replied during a weekly media briefing on Friday.The clarification came in response to a viral post on X claiming that Jaiswal had said, "I have been asked about the funding of the CJP protest many a time.I want to say that our intelligence & investigation reveals there is no foreign funding in it."CJP, an online satirical platform, was formed following a remark by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, in which he described a section of unemployed youth as "cockroaches." The CJI later clarified that he had been misquoted.The allegations of foreign funding have largely been linked to the fact that Abhijit Dipke, who founded the outfit, is a former student of Boston University. Dipke founded CJP in Boston and returned to India in June to lead its demonstrations seeking accountability over the NEET (UG) paper leak in May.The demonstrations peaked on July 20 with the group's "Chalo Sansad" march to Parliament, where protesters faced police action. The crackdown drew criticism from opposition parties, while the police maintained that the protest had turned violent.The 37-day-long agitation culminated in Pradhan's resignation on Saturday afternoon. The CJP called off its stir after the government accepted all its demands.Union minister Pralhad Joshi has been assigned additional charge of Pradhan's ministry of human resource development.

World.title: 'This is a new subject for me': Pralhad Joshi after taking charge as education minister
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Union minister Pralhad Joshi on Sunday assumed charge as the Union education minister, a day after President Droupadi Murmu accepted the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan and assigned him the additional responsibility of the ministry.

Taking charge, Joshi said he was reviewing the ministry's functioning and familiarising himself with the department, describing education as "a new subject" for him.

Speaking to reporters after assuming office, Joshi said

had entrusted him with the responsibility and that he would take time to understand the ministry before making detailed comments.

"The Prime Minister has entrusted me with this responsibility with full confidence.

I was in Karnataka yesterday. I reached here last night and came this morning to take charge. I have assumed charge. I am reviewing all the details here and the decisions that need to be taken. I have been gathering information and trying to understand the functioning of the entire ministry. We had continuous meetings today. This is a new subject for me.

I have taken charge today and held detailed discussions with the senior officers.





It is a very big department, so I will speak to you in detail after I have understood it completely," Joshi said.

Joshi thanks PM Modi, says he accepts responsibility with humility

Soon after taking charge, Joshi shared a message on X thanking Prime Minister Narendra Modi for entrusting him with the Education Ministry.

"Today, I assumed charge as the Union Minister for Education. I am grateful to Hon'ble Prime Minister Shri @narendramodi ji for placing his faith in me and entrusting me with this responsibility," he wrote.

He added, "I accept it with humility and a deep sense of duty."

Assigned additional charge after Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation

Joshi was given charge of the Education ministry on Saturday after President Droupadi Murmu accepted Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation from the Union council of ministers with immediate effect.

According to a Rashtrapati Bhavan statement, Joshi will continue to hold his existing portfolios while also heading the Education Ministry.

"The President of India, as advised by the Prime Minister, has accepted the resignation of Shri Dharmendra Pradhan from the Union Council of Ministers, with immediate effect, under clause (2) of Article 75 of the Constitution of India.

Further, as advised by the Prime Minister, the President has directed that Shri Pralhad Joshi, Cabinet Minister, be assigned the charge of the Ministry of Education, in addition to his existing portfolio," the statement said.

Joshi is currently the Union Minister for Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution and New and Renewable Energy. He has previously served as the Union Minister for Coal, Mines and Parliamentary Affairs.

Poll Vote & Share your view What is the most pressing issue Joshi should address in education? Examination irregularities Improving quality of education Transparency in educational policies 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Change comes amid protests over examination irregularities

The change at the top of the education ministry comes after weeks of nationwide student protests over alleged irregularities in competitive examinations, including the NEET paper leak. Students have been demanding greater transparency, accountability and reforms in the examination system.

Dharmendra Pradhan announced his resignation on Saturday, saying he had submitted it to Prime Minister Narendra Modi in the interest of students and to ensure that the ongoing protests over examination irregularities were not exploited by "anti-national forces."

Meanwhile, the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) announced that it had withdrawn its 36-day-long agitation at Jantar Mantar in "good faith" after Pradhan stepped down from the Union council of ministers and the organisation received assurances from the government on its other demands.

World.title: Can the government take control of foreign-funded assets? FCRA Bill explained
World.content:
India first enacted the FCRA in 1976 during the Emergency era.

The FCRA Bill treats minorities as enemies and is keen on snatching their properties. DMK MP P Wilson

What is FCRA

FCRA... ensures that foreign money enters India through a registered, accountable and disclosed channel... while enabling thousands of organisations to carry out legitimate, impactful work Centre

FCRA restricts foreign funding that may threaten India's sovereignty.

A law that has steadily become stricter

How FCRA steadily become stricter

What the 2026 Bill proposes

FCRA regulates foreign funding that may threaten national interest.

Why the controversy?



FCRA can be used in 9 different sectors

Government sees law as consistent with global trends.

Why Christian organisations are worried

FRCRA like rules in different countries.

Congress echos similar concerns



FCRA myths

The government's response

Govt's clarification on FCRA

In India, the Foreign Contribution Regulation Act (FCRA) is one of those laws that returns to the spotlight every few years â often amid much clamour. But why? The law has repeatedly generated debate over how India should balance scrutiny of overseas funding with the autonomy of NGOs and other civil society organisations.The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026, introduced in the Lok Sabha in March, proposes a new framework for managing foreign contributions and assets when an organisationâs registration is cancelled, surrendered or ceases. The government says the changes are intended to address administrative and legal gaps, while critics question the breadth of the proposed powers.The opposition, however, has argued that the proposed changes hand sweeping powers to the government and could allow it to take control of assets built over decades by charitable organisations.Several church groups, particularly in the Northeast, have argued that the changes could disproportionately affect Christian institutions that use foreign donations for welfare work.So, what exactly is changing, why has the Bill become controversial and what does it mean for thousands of organisations that receive money from abroad?The Foreign Contribution Regulation Act, popularly known as FCRA, governs how individuals, trusts, NGOs, associations and companies in India can receive and use money, securities or other contributions from foreign sources.Administered by the Amit Shah-led home ministry, the law does not prohibit foreign donations. Instead, it lays down who can receive them, how they must be accounted for and where they can be spent.The government has maintained that the purpose behind the tweaking of the legislation is to ensure foreign money enters India through a more transparent and accountable system so that it cannot be diverted towards activities considered âharmfulâ to national interest, democratic institutions or public order.Under the law, any organisation that wants to receive regular foreign funding must obtain an FCRA registration from the home ministry. For those receiving a one-time grant for a specific purpose can seek prior permission instead.Therefore, every rupee received has to pass through a designated bank account, be audited and be reported annually to the government.The law also bars election candidates, legislators, judges, government servants, newspaper editors involved in news reporting and political parties from receiving foreign contributions altogether.The government argues that this is not unique to India. The home ministry has cited foreign-influence registration systems in the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia and Canada to argue that such oversight is not unique to India. However, these systems differ in scope and are not direct equivalents of the FCRAâs broader regulation of foreign contributions.India first enacted the FCRA in 1976 during the Emergency era. Even then, the central concern was âforeign influenceâ over domestic politics and institutions.The framework was significantly overhauled in 2010, when Parliament replaced the old law with the present FCRA. One of the biggest changes was introducing a registration system valid for five years, after which organisations had to renew their licences.In 2020, the law underwent one of its most significant revisions, mandating the organisations receiving foreign funds to route all contributions through a single State Bank of India branch in New Delhi.The ceiling on administrative expenses was reduced from 50 per cent to 20 per cent. Organisations were also barred from transferring foreign funds to other NGOs, while office-bearers had to provide Aadhaar or passport details.Successive amendments have tightened both reporting requirements and operational restrictions. The 2026 Bill extends the framework beyond routine compliance to the management and disposal of assets when an organisationâs registration ends.The headline provision in the Bill concerns organisations whose FCRA registration comes to an end.At present, an organisation may lose its FCRA registration if the government cancels it for violating the law, if the organisation voluntarily surrenders it or if the registration is not renewed.The 2026 Bill formally introduces the concept of a certificate "ceasing" to exist. This would happen if an organisation fails to apply for renewal, misses the renewal deadline or if its renewal application is rejected.That change is significant because the Bill links the end of an FCRA certificate with what happens to foreign-funded assets.The proposed law creates a designated authority to take charge of foreign contributions and assets created using those contributions whenever an organisation's registration is cancelled, surrendered or ceases.Initially, the transfer of assets will be provisional. If the organisation later succeeds in restoring or renewing its registration, the unutilised foreign contributions and assets will be returned.However, if the organisation fails to regain its registration within the prescribed period, the transfer becomes permanent.The designated authority will then have the power to manage those assets, transfer them to central or state government departments or dispose of them through sale. The proceeds from such disposal, along with any remaining foreign contribution, will be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.The Bill also formally defines "key functionaries" who can be held responsible for violations committed by an organisation. These include directors, trustees, partners, office-bearers and others responsible for managing the institution.It requires organisations receiving foreign funds through prior permission to receive and utilise those funds within a prescribed period.Interestingly, the Bill reduces the maximum punishment for violating the Act from five years' imprisonment to one year, a move the government describes as a more proportionate approach to enforcement.Another provision says no investigation into an offence under the Act may be initiated without the prior approval of the central government. The ministry says this would prevent multiple investigations under a central law; the Bill does not specify the criteria or timeframe for granting such approval.As of July 15, 2026, the FCRA portal listed 22,498 cancelled registrations, 15,212 expired registrations and 14,449 active certificates, according to PRS Legislative Research. The government says the lack of a detailed mechanism for handling assets after registration ends has created administrative uncertainty.The government says the designated authority would fill this procedural gap and ensure that permanently vested assets are used for public purposes. Yet it is precisely this argument that has become the biggest point of disagreement.Critics contest that the Bill goes beyond administrative housekeeping and fundamentally changes the relationship between the government and organisations that receive foreign donations. They argue that the proposed provisions could permanently deprive charities of assets they created over decades, even in situations where they no longer depend on foreign funding. That disagreement lies at the heart of the political and religious controversy surrounding the Bill.The central dispute is whether assets created in the past with foreign contributions should vest in the âdesignated authorityâ when an organisation no longer has an active FCRA certificate.That is where the government's reasoning and the opposition's objections diverge. Under the proposed law, assets created using foreign contributions will vest in the âdesignated authorityâ not only when an organisation's registration is cancelled or surrendered but also when it simply ceases because the registration was not renewed or the renewal application was rejected.The government argues this merely formalises an existing principle. It points out that the 2010 Act already provided for vesting of foreign-funded assets when an FCRA registration was cancelled or surrendered.According to the ministry of home affairs, the amendment only creates a detailed statutory framework explaining how those assets should be supervised, managed and disposed of, something that the earlier law did not spell out. It also says the initial vesting will be provisional and assets will be returned if the organisation later restores its registration.Critics, however, believe the practical consequences are far more significant. They argue that an organisation may have built a hospital, school or library years ago with foreign donations but may now be running it entirely through domestic funding. If such an organisation decides not to renew its FCRA registration because it no longer needs foreign contributions, the Bill could still result in those earlier assets vesting with the designated authority.PRS Legislative Research illustrates this concern through a hypothetical example of a healthcare organisation that built a hospital using foreign donations but later operated it entirely with domestic funds. Under the proposed framework, the hospital could still vest in the âdesignated authorityâ if the organisation's registration ceased and was not restored. The authority would then have the power to transfer it to a government department or dispose of it.Critics therefore argue that the amendment effectively creates no practical exit route from the FCRA system. An organisation wishing to retain assets originally built with foreign contributions may feel compelled to continue renewing its registration indefinitely, even if it no longer receives foreign funding. Another concern relates to mixed funding.The Bill says assets created wholly or partly through foreign contributions can vest in the designated authority. In cases where domestic and foreign funds have both been used to build an asset, organisations may apply to recover the identifiable domestic portion. Critics say that, in practice, separating domestic and foreign contributions within a single building or facility may not always be possible.While the existing law provides a mechanism to appeal against cancellation of an FCRA certificate, critics note that neither the Act nor the proposed amendment specifically provides an appeal against refusal to renew a certificate before the assets vest. They also point out that organisations are not guaranteed an opportunity to be heard before renewal is denied.Although the Bill applies uniformly to all organisations, much of the opposition has come from church groups, especially in the Northeast.The Bill is not religion-specific, but church groups, particularly in Mizoram, have been among its most vocal opponents because many affiliated institutions receive foreign donations for welfare projects.Many churches and Christian charitable institutions receive foreign donations to run schools, hospitals, orphanages, homes for persons with disabilities and other welfare projects. Leaders fear that if their FCRA registrations lapse or renewal is denied, properties developed over decades using foreign contributions could eventually pass into government control. These concerns have been particularly strong in Mizoram.Chief minister Lalduhoma held consultations with leaders of the Council of Churches Mizoram and the Mizoram Kohhran Hruaitute Committee, after which it was decided that the provisions of the Bill "cannot be accepted in toto". The state government resolved to prepare a memorandum suggesting changes and seek a meeting with Union home minister Amit Shah.Lalduhoma also said that if the Centre did not accept Mizoram's suggestions, the state's lone Lok Sabha MP from the ruling Zoram People's Movement would oppose the Bill in Parliament.Congressâs Mizoram unit organised protests against the proposed amendment, alleging that Christian institutions would be adversely affected because many charitable organisations in the state depend on overseas donations. Former MP Chella Kumar alleged that the BJP was targeting religious and other minorities while exempting the RSS from the law's purview. Church organisations elsewhere have also stepped up their campaign.Special prayer services were held across several churches following a call by the Joint Action Forum on Minorities to observe a National Day of Fasting and Prayer against the Bill.During one such gathering, DMK MP P Wilson compared the asset provisions with the Enemy Property Act and accused the government of targeting minority institutions. "The Enemy Property Act was enacted to snatch the properties of people who left the country after independence. Similarly, the FCRA Bill treats minorities as enemies and is keen on snatching their properties," he said. A nationwide signature campaign and protests were also announced.The Centre has strongly rejected allegations that the amendment targets any particular religion or seeks to curb legitimate charitable work.According to the home ministry, around 16,200 associations received nearly Rs 22,963 crore in foreign contributions during 2024-25. The ministry cites these figures to argue that the FCRA regulates, rather than prohibits, foreign donations. It says organisations engaged in faith-based welfare activities remain eligible to receive foreign funding and that the law applies equally irrespective of religion, community or ideology. The government has also tried to address concerns over places of worship.The Bill requires the designated authority to preserve the religious character of any permanently vested asset, or part of an asset, that is a place of worship.The government says the framework concerns foreign contributions and assets created from them after an organisationâs registration lawfully ends. The Bill, however, provides that an asset created partly with foreign contributions would initially vest wholly in the Authority, although the organisation may apply for the return of any distinct or ascertainable portion funded from domestic sources.The Centre has further defended restrictions on foreign nationals holding key positions in FCRA-registered organisations, arguing that organisations receiving overseas funding should be managed by individuals with a verified connection to India.Likewise, it said requiring central approval before state-level investigations is appropriate because the FCRA is a central law dealing with foreign funding and national security.

World.title: Kishan Reddy opens Komuravelli Railway station, highlights ₹47,984 crore rail projects
World.content:
Union Minister G. Kishan Reddy said that Komuravelli Railway station would improve rail connectivity to the famous Mallanna temple (Sri Mallikarjuna Swamy) in Siddipet district and provide an affordable travel option for pilgrims and local residents.

Speaking after inaugurating the newly-constructed Komuravelli Punyakshetram Railway Station on the Manoharabad-Siddipet railway line on Sunday, he said the station was constructed at a cost of ₹6 crore, and had been designed with modern features inspired by the architectural grandeur of the Komuravelli temple. “Although the station was not part of the original railway proposals, it was built to meet the growing demand from devotees visiting the shrine,” he said.

The Minister announced that DEMU services operating between Secunderabad and Siddipet would now halt at Komuravelli. As the trains operate with unreserved coaches, travel fares would remain low, making rail travel economical for pilgrims, students, employees and small traders. He said the rail halt was expected to boost spiritual tourism and support local businesses.

Highlighting the progress of the Manoharabad-Kothapalli railway project, Mr. Kishan Reddy said 76 km of the new railway line between Manoharabad and Siddipet had already been completed, establishing rail connectivity towards Karimnagar.

Speaking on railway infrastructure development in Telangana, he said projects worth ₹47,984 crore were currently under various stages of implementation in the State.

The Minister said 40 railway stations in Telangana were being redeveloped under the Amrit Bharat Station Scheme at a cost of more than ₹2,000 crore, with four stations already completed and inaugurated. He also said the long-pending railway manufacturing unit at Kazipet had been established at a cost of ₹521 crore.

Mr. Kishan Reddy said the Railways had also set up 88 stalls across 73 stations in Telangana to provide livelihood opportunities to local artisans, handloom weavers and tribal communities.

Referring to future infrastructure plans, he said three high-speed rail corridors originating from Hyderabad had been proposed, with trains capable of speeds of up to 350 kmph on elevated tracks connecting major capitals.

Union Minister Bandi Sanjay Kumar also spoke. Following the inauguration, Mr. Kishan Reddy travelled by train to Gajwel. Former Governor Bandaru Dattatreya, MPs Chamala Kiran Kumar Reddy, M. Raghunandan Rao and railway officials attended the event.

World.title: MRC commemorates Kargil Vijay Diwas in Coonoor
World.content:
The Madras Regimental Centre (MRC) in Wellington, Coonoor commemorated the 27th anniversary of Kargil Vijay Diwas to pay tribute to the soldiers who laid down their lives during the Kargil War.

Brigadier Krishnendu Das, Commandant, MRC, led the Wreath-Laying Ceremony and Memorial Parade at the War Memorial.

Addressing the gathering, the Commandant recalled the courage, unwavering resolve and indomitable spirit displayed by the bravehearts of Operation Vijay, who overcame formidable odds, treacherous terrain, extreme weather and a determined enemy occupying dominating heights to restore the sanctity of India’s territorial integrity, a press release from the MRC said.

The ceremony concluded with all ranks reaffirming their resolve to uphold the ideals of duty, courage, selfless service and devotion to the Nation, while carrying forward the glorious legacy of the Kargil heroes and remaining ever prepared to safeguard the sovereignty and territorial integrity.

World.title: Sarnath earns UNESCO World Heritage tag, takes India’s tally to 45
World.content:
The ancient Buddhist site of Sarnath in Varanasi was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List during the 48th session of the World Heritage Committee, held in Busan, South Korea. The announcement was made by the committee’s chairperson, Lee Byong Hyun, at the annual conclave on Sunday.

With the inscription of Sarnath, India now has 45 UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

The Uttar Pradesh site has been recognised as a serial property comprising the Chaukhandi Stupa and the Archaeological Remains of Sarnath, which include the preserved archaeological and architectural remains of the ancient Buddhist site.

Sarnath is believed to be the place where Gautama Buddha delivered his first sermon after attaining enlightenment in the 6th century BCE. Also known as Rishipatana, Ishipatana, Mrigadava or the Deer Park, it is regarded as the sacred site where the Buddha met his first disciples, who later spread his teachings on peace and the nature of suffering.

A proud moment for every Indian!



Delighted that Sarnath in Uttar Pradesh has been inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.



Sarnath has a close association with Lord Buddha, whose timeless message of wisdom, compassion and harmony inspires the world.



This recognition… https://t.co/KkdMOg6g0d — Narendra Modi (@narendramodi) July 25, 2026

Reacting to the development, Prime Minister Narendra Modi took to X and posted: “...This recognition celebrates India’s profound civilisational and spiritual heritage. It will also inspire more people across the world to come to Sarnath and connect with the ideals of Lord Buddha.”

Explaining the inscription, UNESCO said, “Sarnath, Varanasi bears witness to the enduring spiritual significance of Sarnath, one of the four principal destinations of Buddhist pilgrimage, established by the Buddha himself, as demonstrated by the large number of religious buildings and other monuments that were built and rebuilt on-site during the many centuries of its existence.”

World.title: Delay in FIR, medical aid alleged in pregnant minor’s POCSO case
World.content:
The alleged delay in registering a case and providing medical care to a pregnant minor girl could have serious health implications for the victim under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, child rights organisations have alleged.

According to the organisations, the girl’s family lodged a complaint at the Nuzvid Rural police station around June 25, 2026, alleging child marriage and offences under the POCSO Act.

The Nuzvid Rural police registered a Zero FIR and referred the girl to an Open Shelter for Girls at Nuzvid in Eluru district the following day.

The management of the Open Shelter produced the girl before the Krishna district Child Welfare Committee (CWC) on June 29. The committee shifted the 14-year-old, who was four months pregnant, to a Child Care Institution (CCI) in NTR district on the same day.

“We alerted the Vissannapet police on June 29 after a 14-year-old pregnant girl in a POCSO case was referred to the CCI. We directed them to register a fresh FIR and follow the prescribed legal and medical procedures,” said CWC member Chandragiri Radha Kumari.

The Vissannapet police, under the NTR Commissionerate, re-registered the case on July 7. The girl was admitted to hospital on July 24.

“We attempted to provide medical assistance to the girl on June 29, but the doctors insisted on an FIR as it was a POCSO case. We conveyed the same to the NTR police, who registered the case only on July 7,” said Krishna district CWC Chairperson K. Suvartha.

Doctors said the foetal growth, haemoglobin level, blood pressure and other vital parameters needed to be monitored regularly to minimise health risks, as the girl was a minor.

“Timely counselling should be provided to the victim on legal and medical aspects, the risks involved and the healthcare required,” said advocate and child rights activist Radha Chandrika.

When contacted, Mylavaram Assistant Commissioner of Police P. Ramachandra Rao, who is investigating the case, said the reasons for the delay, if any, in registering the case and providing medical care would be examined.

“We have arrested the prime accused, and efforts are under way to apprehend the remaining accused,” the ACP said.

World.title: Former Karnataka CM Siddaramaiah announces retirement from electoral politics
World.content:
Former Chief Minister Siddaramaiah has announced his retirement from electoral politics, while asserting that he will continue to remain active in public life and work for the Congress and the people.

Also read | A ‘calm’ Siddaramaiah keeps everyone guessing

Addressing a gathering during the 86th birth anniversary celebrations of former Speaker, the late ‘K.R. Pet’ Krishna, at K.R. Pet town in Mandya district on Saturday (July 26, 2026), the veteran Congress leader said he would not contest the 2028 Assembly elections.

The announcement came after supporters urged him to remain in electoral politics for another decade. Mr. Siddaramaiah, who represents the Varuna Assembly constituency, categorically stated that he would not seek re-election in 2028.

His remarks prompted many in the audience to appeal to him to reconsider the decision. The announcement also disappointed many of his supporters and loyalists in the Congress, several of whom want the 79-year-old leader to continue in active electoral politics.

Mr. Siddaramaiah, Karnataka’s longest-serving Chief Minister after surpassing the record of D. Devaraj Urs, reiterated that he would remain active in politics despite stepping away from electoral contests.

After demitting office as Chief Minister this May to make way for D.K. Shivakumar, Mr. Siddaramaiah had said he would continue serving the people and undertake any responsibility assigned by the Congress high command.

He had also declined the party’s reported offer of a Rajya Sabha seat, saying he was not interested in national politics.

‘Polluted’ and honest politics’

Later, in a Facebook post, Mr. Siddaramaiah said the changing nature of politics had influenced his decision. “Politics has become polluted. Therefore, I have decided not to contest the 2028 Assembly elections. However, I will remain active in politics, stay with the people and continue to support them,” he said.

Recalling his political journey, Mr. Siddaramaiah said he entered public life in 1978 as a member of the Taluk Board and would complete 50 years in politics in 2028. “I have witnessed both victory and defeat, but I have never compromised on my ideology or betrayed my conscience. That gives me immense satisfaction,” he said.
