World.title: ‘Dead in the water’: Navy’s flagship ‘drone ship’ program in doubt
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalDefence ‘Dead in the water’: Navy’s flagship ‘drone ship’ program in doubt Matthew Knott July 26, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A centrepiece of the Albanese government’s push to modernise the navy – a fleet of large, heavily armed warships that can operate with or without sailors on board – has been thrown into doubt after the United States military dumped its plan to develop the vessels. The government insists it is committed to the vision outlined in its 2024 surface fleet review, but defence experts say they expect the plan will need to be abandoned or overhauled. The government announced with much fanfare two years ago that it would boost the firepower of the navy by acquiring six large optionally crewed surface vessels packed with missiles and based on a prototype being developed in the US. A US naval vessel, USV Ranger, on the Pacific Ocean during a training exercise in 2023. But the US navy last year scrapped that program and is instead pursuing a fleet of smaller drone ships that do not have the option of crew members.



Richard Dunley, a senior lecturer in maritime strategy at UNSW, said the US navy’s large unmanned surface vessel program “has been killed”, raising serious questions about the future of Australia’s plan. “The universal assumption was that Australia would piggyback off the US vessel,” he said. “I find it very difficult to see how Australia could do this on our own. “I keep expecting to hear that it’s dead, and I was surprised to see it feature in this year’s national defence strategy.” Former naval officer Jennifer Parker, an expert associate at the Australian National University’s national security college, agreed, saying: “I think we will end up abandoning the idea of large optionally crewed vessels and move to unmanned medium-sized surface vessels in line with the US.”



The vessels would also probably use containerised weapons rather than the vertical launch system envisaged under the government’s plan, she said. The government allocated up to $300 million for optionally crewed surface vessels in its 10-year defence spending plan released in April. But with the vessels estimated to cost around $US250 million ($360 million) each to build, the total cost of the program would ultimately be billions of dollars. Related Article Defence Why the navy is buying a ghost fleet of drone boats for ‘three D’ jobs: Dirty, dull or dangerous “The government is investing $52-$65 billion over the decade to deliver a larger, more lethal surface combatant fleet, through enhancements to strike, air defence and undersea warfare capabilities including six large optionally crewed surface vessels with up to 32 vertical launch system cells to increase the ADF’s maritime long-range strike capability,” a Defence spokesperson said. Greens defence spokesman David Shoebridge called for the government to admit it was proposing to buy a “ghost ship”, describing the affair as the “perfect example of what is wrong with Defence right now.



“The US had a thought-bubble about an experimental and boutique military asset and Labor and the Coalition was so desperate to show their loyalty to the US they immediately signed us up,” he said. “Then when the US spiked the program, without ever consulting Australia, we are left with $300 million attached to a project that is dead in the water. “It’s not just the embarrassment and the incompetence, there is also a huge opportunity cost here in terms of public money and defence resources.” Kamikaze drone boats have played a crucial role in the war in Iran, but these are far smaller and more expendable than the large arsenal ships Australia plans to acquire. Defence firm Austal in November unveiled designs for two new optionally crewed surface vessels – known as the Vantage-class – which it said could meet the Australian navy’s needs.



But military leaders have said they remain committed to developing the vessels with the US. “There is an opportunity for us to realise a really important capability that would take our fleet forwards in terms of its lethality and survivability, but that can’t happen if the US navy don’t commit to the program,” Defence Force vice chief Robert Chipman told Senate estimates hearings in June. “It was tied to the US navy, and there are currently no other options that we’re considering.” Chipman added: “We recognise that there are potential delays to the large optionally crewed vessel, so, yes, we are tracking what the US Navy is saying.” The surface fleet review said the navy would acquire the six vessels “through formal engagement with the United States Navy program as a fast follower”, with an expectation they would enter service in the 2030s and 2040s.



Defence Minister Richard Marles said at the time the vessels would be “exactly based on what has been developed in the United States”, describing the prototype as a “known quantity”. “They have the capacity to operate in an uncrewed fashion, but it is the intention of the Royal Australian Navy to crew these vessels,” he said. Dunley warned at the time that the government was gambling on unproven technology and that the vessels had critics within the US navy. Rear Admiral William Daly, the US navy’s surface warfare requirements director, said last year the large vessels had “walked the path towards exquisite, expensive [and] unpalatable”. The US Naval Institute reported last year that the US military was moving away from optionally crewed vessels because they are considered too costly and complicated.



Unmanned vessels do not require berthing space, galleys, toilets and other features needed to support sailors on board. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: National promises to extend paid parental leave from 26 weeks to 30, if re-elected
World.content:
National has pledged to extend paid parental leave from 26 weeks to 30, if re-elected.

The party is also proposing to revive a policy that allows parents to take some or all of their leave at the same time.

Since 2020, primary carers have been eligible for 26 weeks of paid leave and an additional 26 weeks of unpaid leave.

National has proposed changing the entitlement incrementally, increasing it to 27 weeks in 2027, 28 weeks in 2028, and then 30 weeks in 2029.

Finance spokesperson Nicola Willis said the policy modernised paid parental leave, supporting families to give them more financial breathing space while they took on caregiving responsibilities.

"The birth of a child is an expensive time, as families juggle the costs that come with a new baby while their household income is less than when both parents are in paid work," she said.

Nicola Willis at the announcement on Sunday. TU NATANAHIRA / RNZ

"Extending paid parental leave to 30 weeks will ease that pressure and give more parents the option to stay home with their baby for longer."

Leave is currently capped at $811 a week. National's policy did not propose an increase to that, but Willis said the government had increased the cap each year.

National is also bringing back a previous policy that would allow parents to split their leave.

Christopher Luxon speaking to a child at the announcement. TU NATANAHIRA / RNZ

The party used an example of instead of one parent taking 30 weeks' leave, both parents could take 15 weeks together, or both parents could take 4 weeks together, then one parent could take 10 weeks, and then the other parent could take 12 weeks.

Willis said the current law was restrictive and got in the way of families doing what they thought was best for their babies.

"Whether a dad wants to support mum in the first few weeks after birth, or two caregivers want to share paid leave in overlapping instalments, the choice should sit with families and not restricted by outdated government rules."

The policy would be funded out of Budget operating allowances, costing $27 million in 2027/28, $56.6m in 2028/29, and $119m in 2029/30.

That larger extension is timed to coincide with the forecast return to surplus.

National claims its long-term intention is to increase the entitlement to 40 weeks, but it has not put a timeframe on when it would want to achieve this.

The policy announcement comes as National MPs rally around their colleague Katie Nimon.

The Napier MP's would-be challenger, Stuart Nash, resigned as a New Zealand First candidate, after coming under fire for labelling Nimon as lazy for taking nine months off after having a baby.

MPs do not get paid parental leave. Nimon confirmed she took ten weeks of parental leave and returned to Parliament after six months.

Nimon, who was present at the press conference, said Nash called her on Thursday to apologise.

"He just offered his apology for offending me," she said.

The party insisted it had not timed the announcement off the back of the saga, but Nimon said her views on the policy would be the same regardless of recent events.

"I've said a lot this week, there is no right way of being a working parent. We just need to give people the choice. This policy that we're putting forward is really going to give people that choice. I stand by that, whether what happened this week happened or not."

In 2023, Willis proposed allowing parents to share their leave entitlement so they could take time off together. The member's bill was voted down by Labour at first reading.

Labour then went on to campaign for four weeks' paid parental leave for partners.

National had put forward a member's bill this term to allow for split parental leave, in the name of East Coast MP Dana Kirkpatrick.

It had been unable to get the changes into the coalition agreement or pass them as a government this term. Willis said the responsibility for parental leave rested with the Workplace Relations and Safety Minister, ACT's Brooke van Velden.

"I think it's a shame that it wasn't prioritised within the minister's programme for this term, and we are really keen as a National Party to see this done."

ACT leader David Seymour defended his colleague, saying van Velden had not worked on parental leave flexibility because she had not been asked to.

"She hasn't been asked by the National Party to do that. It's not in their coalition documents. They didn't try and negotiate it into their agreement. I was disappointed because I think people want to see the coalition pointing to what it's achieved rather than pointing fingers at each other."

Seymour said the timing of the announcement felt political, given the events of the past week.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins asked why National should be trusted now.

"They have had three years to make life easier for Kiwis and support families, but have instead cut Best Start support for parents, reduced funding for school lunches, cut women's pay, and failed to tackle the cost of living."

Hipkins said Labour would have a "comprehensive" paid parental leave policy, which it would set out in due course.

Green Party co-leader Marama Davidson said National's policy was too little, too late.

"The only time that government cares about women is when it is polling low. We have seen them trash the lives of women, whether it's through cancelling pay equity claims for hundreds of thousands of women, whether it's in keeping wage growth low, because that impacts disproportionately women. This government made decisions to keep one in seven children in poverty. That is, children and their mothers."

Last month, National announced a policy to continue paying the government KiwiSaver contribution to people on paid parental leave.

Some parents online called National's promise to extend paid parental leave a "lolly scramble".

Many questioned why National would wait until after an election to implement much needed help, and more said the policy was not enough.

A few commenters on Facebook suggested that increasing the payments rather than the length of the leave would help families more.

A couple said they had had to go to work earlier because they could not afford to live on PPL payments.

Lisa, Wellington mum of a two-and-a-half-year old, said the policy was a step in the right direction but was missing the bigger issue: the cost of early childhood education (ECE).

"I know parents that are paying upwards of $1500 a fortnight for two children just to keep their jobs, or else they're just opting to leave their careers," she said.

She said help with childcare costs would have left her better off financially than more time off work.

"We constantly hear Christopher Luxon saying he wants to get people back to work, but you're getting people back to work who are then having to spend half their salary on ECE fees just so they can go to work. It's just this awful cycle."

She said the high fees were also keeping people from having more children.

World.title: Commonwealth Games: Pacific hope for medals in bowls and boxing
World.content:
There is hope that the Pacific Island contingent at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow will be able to win medals in bowling and boxing.

Top Fijii men's singles player Rajnesh Parasad is the best bet for a medal in the bowls, following his early three round wins so far.

Prasad claimed his first win on Friday morning, when he beat England's top bowler Sam Tolchard in a tie-break, after the two players were tied 1-1 at the end of two sets.

Tolchard won the prestigious World Singles Champion of Champions title in November 2022 in New Zealand, and claimed the top title at the Bowls World Cup in November 2025.

Prasad then defeated Jamaica's Robert Simpson 2-0 in clean sets in his second game. He won 12-1 in the first and 6-5 in the second to wrap the game up.

He also claimed his third win on Sunday morning, taking the tie-break against Scotland's Jason Banks, after the duo had ended the game tied with a set each to their names.

In boxing, male boxers Kiribati's Eriu Temakau won his men's 55kg bout in a split-points decisions against Guernsey's Thomas Teers.

Papua New Guinea's James Paul also got through his first fight, winning a points decision as well over Bahrains Rashield Williams.

Tonga's Josh Tonga is the third Pasifika boxer to win his first bout, defeating Trinidad and Tobago's Jeremiah Thomas in the men's 80kg division.

The three Pasifika boxers will feature in the Round of 16.

Tonga told the media after his win he was excited and looks forward to his next bout.

"Amazing," he said.

"Words can't explain, the atmosphere is insane, and our team is behind me, coaches, families and friends watching as well, it's incredible.

"The game plan was to keep my distance, take little wee steps, keeping it simple in general."

In other results:

Bowls - Women's Pairs

Norfolk Islands pair of Ellie Dixon and Christie Jones beat Cook Islands duo Fa'amanatu Vasie Ngatoko-Oila and Teokotai Rahui Jim 2-0, winning 8-3 and 10-1 in both sets.

Cook Islands returned strong in the second game of the weekend, when they defeated Falkland Islands 2-0, winning 8-2 and 8-2 in the two sets.

Norfolk Islands also did the same when they beat the Jersey pair 2-0 in their clash, winning 7-1 and 7-2..

Niue's Catherine Papani and Christine Ioane lost 2-0 to the Northern Ireland pair of Chloe Wilson and Shauna O'Neill. Northern Ireland won both sets 9-1 and 11-0.

They also lost 2-0 to Singapore, losing both sets 12-4 and 11-2 and went down to Zambia as well.

The Tonga pair of paris Baker and Milika Nathan dropped game two after their first round win, this time losing on tie-break to England. The two teams battled to winning a set each before England took the tie-break 1-0.

They also lost their third game, going down too on tie-break to India in another tight game.

Fijian pair Litia Tikoisuva and Losalini Tukai went down 2-0 to Wales in their second game. Wales won both sets 8-0 amd 5-3.

They did win their next game, beating Kenya 1.5-0.5, claiming the first set 7-2 before the two teams fought to a 5-all draw in the second set.

Bowls - Men's Singles

Royden Aperau of Cook Islands defeated Taylor Greechan of Jersey in a tie-break. Greechan won the first set 5-4 before Aperau claimed the second 9-2 and then won the tie-break 2-0.

He was unlcuky on Sunday morning when he lost 2-0 to Isle of Man's Mark McGreal.

But then came back strong to win 2-0 against Guernsey's Jason Greenslade.

Tonga's Liam Hall won two games after having lost in the first round, defeating Niue's Frederrick Tafatu 2-0. Hall won 11-4 and 8-4 to secure a clean record in that game.

He then defeated South Africa's Wayne Rittmuller in his third game, taking the tie-break in that clash.

Niue's Tafatu, on the other hand, took New Zealand's Shannon McIlroy to the wire in their match before losing on tie-break, after both players had claimed a set each in normal play.

However, he lost to Northern Ireland's Gary Kelly in the tie-break when the two had fought to winning a set each. Kelly took the tie-break 1-0 to claim victory.

Boxing

Fiji's Ben Maukakala lost his first fight and exited the Games after the referee stopped the contest in round two of his men's 65kg clash against New Zealand's Connor Campbell.

Nauru's Vi-J Tebouwa also suffered a loss against Scotland's Leo Church in his opening bout of the same division.

However, not all was good for Vanuatu's Ricksen Nomleas who lost in the first round against England's Ellis Trowbridge and Solomon Islands' Clinton Tetekana, who lost to Bangladesh's Md Rakib Hossan. Both Nomleas and Tetekana were saved by the referee who stpped in to stop their fights.

PNG's Petronella Nokenoke lost by points to England's Lucy Kings-Wheatley in the women's 60kg contest.

On Sunday morning, mixed results were again recorded by Pasifika boxers.

Niue's Phoenix Gataua lost on points to Botswana's Treasure Moremi, followed by loses also to Solomon Islands duo Lio Dicks and Max Makana, Fiji's Jone Davule, Niue's Kalani Anitelea-Launiu and Samoa's Dee Ioapo.

3x3 Basketball

In the women's competition, Fiji defeated Cayman Islands 16-6 in their opening Pool A game but lost 16-14 to Kenya in their second match and Australia 21-3 in their third game.

Tonga beat Scotland 12-10 in their Pool B opener and Papua New Guinea in their third game, but lost 21-8 to New Zealand in their second match.

PNG lost 22-6 to New Zealand and 21-8 to Singapore as well in their Pool G games.

In the men's competition, the Fiji men's team lost 21-16 to Malaysia, 21-13 to England but beat Jamaica 21-13 in their three Pool B games.

The Games media said there was a lovely moment from Tongan sisters Mele Finau and Lesila Finau, who helped the Pacific nation to a surprise 12-10 win over hosts Scotland in their opening match of the Women's 3x3 Basketball, with younger sibling Mele saying:

"She has been my role model for the past 20-something years. It has been great having her by my side and representing our country together. Sibling love can be a bit of tough love at times but it definitely helps on the court."

Swimming

Cook Islands' Carter Makira finished sixth in the heat two of the men's 200 metres individual medley, while Samoa's Christian Toia was eighth in heat three.

Nafanua Hamilton was placed sixth in the women's 200m backstroke heats. She also placed eigth in the women's 200m freestyle.

In the women's 50 metres butterfly heats PNG pair Jhnayali Tokome-Garap and Roxanne Kirarock finished third and fourth respectively in heat one, while teammate Joanna Chew was fourth in heat two, ahead of Vanuatu's Loane Russet, who was at fifth spot.

Fiji's Anahira McCutcheon finished fourth in heat five, while Samoa's Paige Schendelaar-Kemp was eighth in that heat.

PNG's Thomas Chan won heat one of the men's 100m backstroke, while Cook Islands' Carter Makira was third in heat two, ahead of Fiji's Don Younger in fourth.

Heat three saw Fiji's Samuela Yalimaiwai in fifth position while Samoa's Christian Toia was eighth.

In the men's 50m freestyle heats, Tonga's Finau Ohuafi finished first in heat 3 ahead of Vanuatu's Leo Lebot in second, while Fiji's Reuben Taylor won heat 4, which also had PNG's Josh Tarere in fourth and his countryman Thomas Chen in seventh.

Fijian pair David Young and Hansel McCaig both competed in heat 8, with Young finishing second while McCaig was eighth.

The women's 100m backstroke also saw a number of Pasifika swimmers, which included PNG's Joanna Chen claiming third in heat one, Samoa's Hamilton being second in heat two, with Cook Ilands' Mia Laban at fifth.

Netball

Tonga's Tala were thrashed 99-38 by Australia in their opening Pool A clash on Saturday night.

New Zealand defeated Scotland 74-44 in their opener.

The Games continue daily until 2 August.

As of 5pm on Sunday (NZT), Australia led the medal tally with 12 gold, five silver and five bronze.

World.title: Hospitals builds adopt new way to put digital infrastructure systems in place
World.content:
Two big hospital builds are adopting a new way of getting complex digital infrastructure systems put in place, with a tweak.

Whangārei and Nelson builds are adapting what the Dunedin redevelopment did when it hired a digital system integrator.

They are tweaking it slightly by putting the integrator under the main contractor instead directly with Health New Zealand.

Health NZ says getting hospital IT done this way recognises what a big job it is.

"It also aims to avoid perpetuating legacy technical issues by ensuring that contemporary, resilient digital infrastructure, aligned to Health New Zealand digital standards, is implemented on the major hospital build programmes," it said.

It was working successfully in Dunedin, it added.

Its tender alerting companies it will be hiring, invites them to join a list of pre-qualified suppliers for when the job is let for real.

It says that list may be used for other similar hospital projects in future.

World.title: Tottenham Hotspur beat Auckland FC 2-0 in pre-season friendly
World.content:
Tottenham Hotspur have beaten Auckland FC 2-0 in an entertaining pre-season friendly match at Eden Park in Auckland today.

Spurs, on a southern tour that includes two games in Australia, held a 1-0 lead at halftime, and doubled their tally in the second.

Spurs dictated early and their first goal to Dane Scarlett was due reward. It resulted from a terrific cross from Archie Gray to Manor Solomon who fired a shot which Auckland goalie Michael Woud stopped but couldn't hold and Scarlett pounced.

Auckland had their chances, and a Logan Rogerson pass found Sam Cosgrove late in the half, but goalie Brandon Austin was able to hold out his shot.

Both teams made numerous changes in the second half, with Spurs introducing some of their best talent..

One of them, Brazilian forward Richarlison, scored midway through the spell after a brilliant run from Mathys Tel set him up.

The match attracted a crowd of around 40,000 and was a boost for Spurs fans after they just survived Premier League relegation last season.

A-League victors Auckland were outclassed on a wet day, but will surely benefit from a game against Premier League opposition.

World.title: NZ Warriors scrape home with lucky win over Eels
World.content:
The Warriors have made it three wins from four matches with a frantic 14-12 victory over the Parramatta Eels in their NRLW clash Sydney today.

They had to do it in the hard way, after being down 12-4 in the 40th minute.

They fought back to a take a two point lead but then things went awry as they lost a player to the bin with four minutes to go and the Eels started to make big inroads against a struggling defence.

Dane Scarlett scores and celebrates his goal for Tottenham Hotspur against Auckland FC at Eden Park, Auckland, 26 July 2026. Photosport.nz

In the dying seconds the Eels looked to have stolen the game as Zali Fay went over in the left corner after an overlap but the officials ruled the final pass was forward and the home side's celebrations turned to despair.

The Warriors lacked the fluency of their play in their 42-4 win over the North Queensland Cowboys last weekend against opponents looking for their first win of the season.

But Patricia Maliepo's try in the 51st minute got them back on track, and Tysha Ikenasio handed the Eels a double blow just three minutes later.

The score stayed at 14-12 there, with the Warriors scraping in for a fortunate win.

World.title: Christchurch Catholic Diocese unveils plans for new $80m Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament
World.content:
The design of Christchurch's new $80 million Catholic cathedral has been unveiled.

The Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament is being built on the Barbadoes Street site of the 1905 original, which was demolished in 2020 after suffering irreparable damage in the 2010 and 2011 earthquakes.

The damaged Christchurch Catholic Basilica, 2019. Peter Fleming

The Catholic Diocese of Christchurch wants to raise $16m from parishioners to help fund the project.

In a pastoral letter on Sunday, Bishop Michael Gielen appealed to Catholic families in Canterbury and on the West Coast to financially contribute.

Gielen announced in 2024 the cathedral would return to the diocese's traditional home on Barbadoes Street and that it would retain the name Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament.

A design rendering for Christchurch's new Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament. Supplied / Catholic Diocese of Christchurch

He said that in the two years since significant work had been undertaken to develop the design in partnership with the architecture firm Warren and Mahoney.

"When I arrived in the diocese four years ago, one of the questions I was most often asked was: 'What is happening with the cathedral?'. That question revealed something profound, the deep love our people have for their Mother Church," Gielen said.

"Over these past four years, through listening, prayer and discernment, that shared vision has taken shape."

"It is an ancient design, a Romanesque and Gothic hybrid model. So that's drawing on the best of humanity's learnings over the centuries, that's beautiful to connect to that."

A design rendering for Christchurch's new Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament. Supplied / Catholic Diocese of Christchurch

Gielen believed people would see in the design: "a cathedral that glorifies God, that serves as a beacon of faith in our city, that responds to the realities of the present day".

The diocese's cathedral campaign manager, Tony Brazier, said the project had an $80m budget that would cover the 800-seat cathedral, the attached perpetual adoration chapel and the Te Rangimarie community centre.

Brazier said about $45m of the funds needed to build the cathedral would come from insurance proceeds and the sale of diocesan assets.

Of the $35m required through fundraising, more than $19m had already been found, he said.

The proposed site of the Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

"Bishop Michael is emulating what Bishop Grimes did, inviting every Catholic family to make a sacrificial offering to build our new cathedral," he said

Gielen said he had heard from many people who had a sense of pride that their grandparents or great-grandparents helped fund the construction of the original Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament.

"It's now our turn to answer the ancient call to build something that will last for generations," he said.

The Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament, Christchurch, as it looked in 2005. Wikimedia Commons

"I have been struck by the generosity of people who recognise what a sign of hope our cathedral will be for Christchurch and our region. That generosity has been seen around New Zealand and from people of other faith traditions."

The diocese said that when half of the remaining $16m had been raised, the project would move towards final preparations for construction.

"We're only $8m short of pressing go on the build, so I'm very hopeful that people will get in behind it," Gielen said.

The cathedral will be the first new Catholic cathedral in New Zealand in 120 years.

Lead architect for the cathedral, Joseph Hampton, said he was honoured to be involved with the project.

"My great-great-great-grandfather donated to the first cathedral built, and my family has been involved in the parish throughout the years," he said.

"We received a really rich brief from the bishop and his amazing advisory group, so from there we started with master planning and making sure we arranged the site in a way that allows the campus to feel alive for the next 20, 50, 150 years.

"It's a cathedral that's grounded in tradition but built for Christchurch today."

World.title: ACT campaigns to close the Pharmac funding gap
World.content:
The ACT Party is proposing to increase the proportion of the health budget spent on Pharmac by one percent a year, to bring New Zealand in line with Australia and closer to the OECD average.

The policy would see Pharmac's budget rise to 12 percent of the total health spend by 2033.

Currently, New Zealand spends 4.9 percent of the health budget on medicines, well below the OECD average of 13.3 percent.

ACT leader David Seymour, who currently holds ministerial responsibility for Pharmac, told RNZ he had spent the last three years in government trying to increase Pharmac's budget.

"Pharmac is punished for being tougher on its costs than anyone else in the healthcare system. We need to give them a break."

The uplift, he said, would enable Pharmac to fund more medicines on its Options for Investment list.

There were currently 139 applications on the wishlist, which are all pharmaceuticals that Pharmac would fund if it had the money to.

In the 2026 Budget, the health system received a $1.5 billion funding uplift, but Seymour said Pharmac got just $13.5 million.

He was hoping for cross-party support for the policy.

"It is actually an achievable, realistic, and timely way to approach a problem that everyone admits, but no one has ever quite got on top of."

Despite being the minister, he had not pitched the idea to his coalition partners.

"I have asked for more modest increases in medicines funding, which have been rejected. The logic that I'm producing now, I believe, is unassailable as a way of persuading anyone who's in government - and let's be really honest, between now and 2033 there'll probably be several different people in government - this is a logic that anyone can sign up to."

Seymour said he was proud of the work he had done with Pharmac and MedSafe to get more medicines, but it had only gone so far.

"You could see this as a final jigsaw piece in the work that I've done over the last three years."

At the lower end of ACT's costings, it used the Treasury's 2025 Long-term Fiscal Model, while at the upper end it applied the Treasury's 2025 Overlapping Generations model's projected health-spending share to nominal GDP forecasts and projections.

This meant in 2027/28, overall health spending would be between $33.4 billion and $36.6 billion. With the medicines share increasing from 5 percent to 6 percent, it would put medicine expenditure between $2 billion and $2.2 billion.

By 2033/34, with a projected health expenditure of $44.9 billion to $51 billion, and a 12 percent medicines share, medicine expenditure would be between $5.4 billion and $6.1 billion.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins was supportive of the policy, saying Labour wanted to see health funding focused on preventative healthcare.

"Increasing funding for medicines, particularly where those medicines are focused on prevention, that's a very good thing."

National's health spokesperson Simeon Brown said the party would have more to say on its election health policy soon.

World.title: Greens unveil election manifesto at packed AGM in Auckland
World.content:
The Green Party have unveiled their election manifesto to a packed-out annual general meeting at an auditorium in south Auckland.

The 43-page document - which is developed by party members - sets out the party's priorities for the 2026 general election, and includes policies on climate action, democracy, Te Tiriti o Waitangi, incomes and digital technology.

Co-leader Marama Davidson said manifesto contains issues that needed attention "now and over the next three years".

"We're going to make sure that people have affordable lives, that we protect nature to be healthy, [and] that we return politics to being honest to make decisions for all of us."

"We will tax the super-rich and address corporate greed so that we can invest that back into the services that people rely on."

Davidson said the manifesto showed the party's position on "broad issues" and signalled some longer-term ambitions too.

The party also unveiled their campaign slogan: "For All of Us".

Green co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said the slogan was for both supporters and people the party "don't know and even those we don't like".

"What we believe, very fundamentally, is that we are not just here to fight for the basic human rights to access food and healthcare and shelter and education and job opportunities for the people that we know and like, but also for the people we don't know and even those we don't like."

The manifesto launch followed a call from the party for a one-year pause on new AI data centre consents until stricter national rules are in place.

In March, Singapore-based company Datagrid was given resource consent to develop a new $3.5 billion data centre in Southland.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon called the Green Party "alarmist" and said data centres were critical to adding value to the country's economy.

But Swarbrick told the AGM at Auckland University of Technology's Manukau campus that AI data centres did not offer long term employment.

"Experience overseas has shown AI data centres extract local water supplies and give back sludge. They extract an enormous toll on the power grid, driving up electricity prices for regular people and local industry."

"They extract power, they extract water, and they extract profit." she said

Swarbrick took aim at "powerful men" who she said made decision to increase profits for the few.

"They tell us it's inevitable, that we have to suck it up. We're told this is 'growth'."

"They promise that if those companies can just extract a bit more, we'll surely get something back."

World.title: Fozball and finals on the brink as Cronulla maul Manly
World.content:
Manly's hopes of a fairytale NRL finals berth are on life support after an insipid 48-12 loss to Cronulla, who appear genuine premiership contenders.

The Sea Eagles suffered their worst defeat of the Kieran Foran era as Sharks halves Nicho Hynes and Braydon Trindall lit up Brookvale Oval.

The 10th-placed Sea Eagles (9-10) have a losing record for the first time since round six and must win at least four of their last five regular-season games to play finals.

They are four competition points out of the top eight and face top-eight sides Newcastle, the Dolphins and Warriors on the run home.

It's been quite the fall from grace for the Sea Eagles, who rose from the doldrums and won eight of 10 games immediately after Foran replaced Anthony Seibold.

Manly have since lost five of six, and for the first time since club legend Foran became coach in March, they were never in the contest on Sunday.

The Sea Eagles' playmakers gave away four seven-tackle sets with poor kicks.

Reuben Garrick sprayed the kick-off out on the full after the Sharks' fourth try and put the visitors in place for Sione Katoa to score their fifth only minutes before the half.

Tom Trbojevic's replacement Lehi Hopoate had an afternoon to forget at fullback, notably spilling a regulation Hynes kick directly ahead of the Sharks' third try.

The fourth-placed Sharks have won eight from their last nine games and look ready to take the leap from good to great in Craig Fitzgibbon's fifth season as coach.

So long a lightning rod for criticism, halfback Hynes is playing as well as he has since winning the Dally M Medal in 2022.

He embarrassed the Manly middle barging over for the Sharks' fourth try and sent a bullet-like pass for Ronaldo Mulitalo's second try just after the break.

Hynes dummied through rookie five-eighth Joey Walsh, who had a difficult day, and then passed inside for Sifa Talakai to score in the second half.

He also kicked a career-best 26th consecutive goal and finished the afternoon with three line breaks.

Trindall's suspect ball to Teig Wilton gave Cronulla their opening try, before the five-eighth floated a lovely cut-out pass for Mulitalo's first.

He kicked past Hopoate for KL Iro to cross with 15 minutes to play.

Just before halftime, the Sea Eagles lost second-rower Ben Trbojevic to his second game-ending head knock in as many appearances.

Earlier, the makings were all there for another devastating Gold Coast loss, but coach Josh Hannay has credited the Titans' ongoing evolution for their slashing 38-18 win over St George Illawarra.

With the Dragons celebrating co-captain Clint Gutherson's 250th NRL game on Sunday afternoon, the permanent signing of coach Dean Young and Old Boys' Day to boot, the visitors had to overcome an early deficit to secure consecutive wins for the first time in the Hannay era.

Gold Coast's 20-point win allowed them to leapfrog three other clubs, and out of the competition's bottom four for the first time since their round-eight bye, and all but confirmed the Dragons' maiden wooden spoon.

"When you're coming into an environment like this, it felt like we were walking into a trap with them having so much to play for, so I just loved how we went about it," Hannay said.

"We have had some tight losses and haven't had a lot of reward at different times. There have been a few instances where we have had a level game at halftime and we'd flinch in the second half. I feel like this group, little by little, are growing.

"We're fully aware of where we're at, the journey we're on and that there's going to be some hard lessons. They have had to learn a lot on the run these guys and they're growing exponentially."

World.title: Lion's 'stupid action' sparks war of words as Nasiah magic inspires Saints
World.content:
Brisbane defender Ty Gallop faces an anxious wait on the match review officer after a contentious incident in the second quarter of the Lions' heavy win over Port Adelaide at the Gabba.

The emerging Gallop had rolled Mitch Georgiades in a heavy tackle, but while the Power key forward's head did not hit the turf, it was what happened next that raised eyebrows.

As the Lions swept the ball downfield, Gallop appeared to lift Georgiades by the jumper before slamming him back into the turf head first.

While Georgiades played out the game uninjured, he was returning from an earlier concussion against St Kilda in round 18 after being knocked out in a heavy mid-air collision.

The incident spurred a defensive reaction from both coaches after the match, with Port's Josh Carr saying Gallop's actions were the mark of a team that played its football on the edge.

"It wasn't a great look, but I'm on the other side of it," he said.

"They're a team that plays tough and pushes the limits. We got the free kick, so we got rewarded. There's not much more to say."

Carr said Georgiades was unaffected by the incident after the game.

But the coach's words spurred a response from his counterpart Chris Fagan, who said he hadn't seen the incident.

Asked if he agreed with Carr's assessment that his team played on the edge, Fagan said: "That's his opinion. He's allowed to have it.

"You don't be one of the better teams of the competition if you don't play a hard physical brand.

"That's what we do. I don't think we do it unfairly. I think we brought good pressure today."

Brisbane Lions great Alastair Lynch was also unimpressed by Gallop's actions, citing Georgiades's history with concussions as well.

"That's just a stupid action. We don't want to see that," he said on Fox Footy's coverage.

"Mitch [Georgiades] has had some problems with concussion and we don't want to see actions like that."

Fagan said he had yet to view a replay of the incident.

"It's interesting that Josh has had a chance to watch it; I haven't. He's not as busy as what I am," he said.

Fagan said he was hopeful defender Darcy Gardiner was available next week should Gallop be suspended.

"It's not really up to me; it's up to what the match review mob [and] what they decide," he said.

In Sunday's second match, St Kilda ran out 13.15 (93) to 8.14 (62) winners over North Melbourne as Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera finished with 46 disposals and four goals.

AAP

World.title: Tim Tszyu beats Errol Spence Jr by unanimous decision
World.content:
Tim Tszyu has beaten Errol Spence Jr in a blockbuster non-title boxing match in Sydney by unanimous decision, with the American great retiring in the ring post-fight.

All three judges scored the bout in favour of the Australian, 118-110, 117-111, 117-111, who moves to a 28-3 professional record, while handing Spence his second consecutive defeat.

Tszyu controlled the middle portion of the contest, marching down the former champion, who looked as rusty as you might expect from a man who has spent three years out of the ring.

"I had sleepless nights … how am I gunna feel facing a legend like that," Tszyu said in the ring.

"I understand why he is one of the greats.

"I wanna win a world title, but beating a great like Errol Spence tops any world title for me."

Tim Tszyu controlled the middle portion of the fight against Errol Spence Jr. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

Spence, a former unified world welterweight world champion, had not fought since 2023 when he suffered the first defeat of his professional career against Terrence Crawford, who was ringside for the contest.

In his time out the ring, Spence suffered a car crash that could have claimed his career, if not more.

But Tszyu, the larger man despite fighting at welterweight for the first time, was able to use his size to dictate the fight, marching down Spence and cutting off the ring.

Spence gave Tszyu's body a thorough examination in the opening rounds off the back of a clever jab and canny left hook, the 36-year-old ran out of steam as the fight went on.

There were signs throughout that the former WBA, WBC and IBF champion was not he same fighter that he used to be, looking unsteady and unsure on his feet.

As such, it was no real surprise that he revealed in the ring that he would not be continuing his fighting career.

"Congratulations to Tim, Jeff Fenech, it was a good showing by Tim" Spence said.

"I asked a lot of questions for myself. Now it's time to go home with my family and start a new life.

"I got my faculties intact, my money is good, it's working for itself, so everything's good.

"Now it's time to go home and life that family life."

It was all smiles between the two combatants after the fight. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

Tszyu, who admitted to some dark thoughts about his career ahead of this fight, credited his new coach, Jeff Fenech, for forcing him to stick to his game plan.

"The two greats I'm trying to replicate are Kostya Tszyu and Jeff Fenech.

"If I can get half as good as them, hey, I'll be sleeping as a great man.

Earlier, Commonwealth Games silver medallist and 2024 Paris Olympian Callum Peters earned a stoppage victory over Argentinian Luis Antonio Tejeda.

Tokyo Olympian Paulo Aokuso also secured victory via a spectacular 10th round knock out win despite struggling through the middle rounds against unbeaten Dominican Republic fighter Luis Antonio Tejeda.

In the co-main, veteran lightweight Paul Fleming was well beaten by unbeaten youngster Ahmad Reda via unanimous decision.

Paris Olympian Tina Rahimi beat Sacha Ryan Dryden for her first professional win as well.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

World.title: No more tears left to cry as Godwin goes from hell to the mountaintop
World.content:
Four years ago, Georgia Godwin was at the peak of her powers as she led Australia to silver in the women's team final at the Birmingham Commonwealth Games.

She performed all four of the apparatus and had the highest score in three of them.

This time around, her first two rotations were just OK, aided by brilliant performances by Kate McDonald, whose 14.200 was the best uneven bars score of the day; and Breanna Scott on beam.

They backed it up on the floor, with first Scott, then McDonald posting the day's second-best scores on the apparatus.

Godwin was a picture of composure. (Getty Images: Naomi Baker)

Then Godwin reminded the world of her class with a stunning routine that earned her a 13.350 and left Australia in top spot with only the vault to come.

"There was a lot going through my head before that floor routine and the girls before me absolutely nailed their floors. I just really wanted to help the team and with all of that head noise and all of that pressure I just started feeling a bit overwhelmed," she said.

"So before I started floor, I went to my plans and grounded myself and I was so happy for that to be my first floor routine back at a big international event."

The moment her music faded out, the emotions came rushing into Godwin and out onto her face.

Georgia Godwin burst into tears immediately after her floor routine. (Getty Images: Owen Humphreys/PA Images)

Some mixture of pride and relief. Then the tears as she embraced every member of the team who had helped her get back.

The Achilles she tore two and a half years ago hadn't just held up, it had propelled her and her team towards almost certain gold in Glasgow.

Athletes often talk of resilience gained and lessons learned through adversity, but sometimes it just sucks to be unceremoniously kicked off the mountaintop, have your livelihood threatened and independence taken away.

"I'm gonna be completely honest, it's been a horrible, horrible road back," she said.

"My support team has been absolutely amazing, but the mental challenges I've had to go through have been the hardest I've been through in my life.

"But I want to finish this sport on my own terms and I wanted to do one more big event with these amazing girls.

The village got Georgia Godwin through hell. (Getty Images: Matthias Hangst)

"I've said it before and I'll say it over and over again, but it takes a village and I'm so lucky to have my special village."

That village includes her parents, who were in the stands to watch, her teammates, her coaches, physio, trainers, and of course puppy Remy.

Unsurprisingly, there were times when she thought she wouldn't be able to get back.

Too old, too sore, too hard. Just all too much.

It was too much again on Saturday night at the Glasgow International Arena.

The energy was high from the Australians throughout the final. (Getty Images: Naomi Baker)

Asked about her mindset as she stepped onto the floor, the emotions came for her again.

"I'm gonna have no tears left by the end of this," she laughed.

A solid 20 seconds of overwhelm later, she said she wasn't performing for herself but those dozens, hundreds of people who have helped her get back on the mat, the bars, the vault and the floor.

Five seconds later she was laughing about becoming Australia's most decorated female gymnast, and joking at the expense of Allana Slater.

It was another reminder of her ability to compartmentalise, albeit slightly less impressive than when she managed to compose herself after the ultimate release of sticking that floor routine to pull off a similarly superb 13.550 vault.

In a competition where they won gold by 1.1 point, a half misstep or misalignment could have seen the ultimate goal slip through her fingers again.

Georgia Godwin has returned to the top of the world. (Gety Images: Naomi Baker)

"My emotions don't come up very often but when they do I'm very good at suppressing them if I've got a job to do," she said.

"I think it's so important to feel your emotions but there's also a time and place, so I took the moment, got myself into a quiet corner and just laid down and tried to calm myself back down and did the job."

Job done, but not really.

Still ahead of her in Glasgow are gold medal defences in the all-around and vault finals, and a floor final.

But today isn't about any of that.

Today is about reminding her who she is, what she can do, and why she does it.

"I think everything is all good," she said.

"We can move on and I've really taken a step today."

World.title: Quick hits: Photographer watches partner win gold, tiny nation makes history
World.content:
The partner of an Australian gold medallist nervously watches his final while working on the pool deck, while a swimmer loses her cap in the middle of a race.

Here are the quick hits from day two of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Picture perfect moment

Sam Williamson (right) celebrates with his partner Linnea Lindberg after winning gold. (Reuters: Phil Noble)

Spare a thought for Sam Williamson's partner Linnea Lindberg.

As Williamson powered to an emotional victory in the men's 100m breaststroke final, Lindberg was forced to nervously watch on in her professional capacity.

You see, Lindberg is working at the Comm Games as an accredited photographer.

Williamson joked after his final he was not sure about the quality of any snaps she took during his race.

"I can't imagine they'll be good," Williamson joked to the Seven Network.

"I reckon she's got more tears in her eyes than I do at the moment … if we get one good photo from tonight, it's all worth it."

Sam Williamson (left) and Linnea Lindberg caught the eye of poolside photographers. (Reuters: Andrew Couldridge)

Williamson and Lindberg were able to catch up and celebrate on the pool deck, much to the delight of the other photographers working at the swimming.

2. Aussie loses swimming cap

Sienna Toohey lost one of her swimming caps during her 100m breaststroke heat. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

No doubt Sienna Toohey thought she was ready for any challenge thrown at her at the Commonwealth Games.

That was until one of her swimming caps fell off mid-race during the heats of the women's 100m breaststroke.

"I got to the end [of my heat] and they [officials] were like, 'Has anyone lost a cap?', and I was like, 'Yeah, that's me,'" Toohey said.

She said officials told her she could dive back in the pool and retrieve the cap, but there was only one problem.

"I couldn't find it anywhere in the pool," Toohey said.

"I was thinking: 'I've got to get this cap back, I need it for tonight.'"

Toohey eventually found the cap, with the Tollcross International Swimming Centre crowd giving her a warm round of applause.

The "wardrobe malfunction" did delay the heats program, although no-one seemed bothered.

For the record, Toohey won her heat in a time of 1:07.30.

3. Diamonds put out call to Outlander star

Scottish actor Sam Heughan is in demand. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot)

The Australian netball team has laid down a challenge to Scottish actor Sam Heughan.

The Diamonds want to meet up with Heughan, who plays Jamie Fraser in the Outlander series, after he was spotted at a Scottish team training session.

Kiera Austin and Courtney Bruce are among the Diamonds players who have taken to Instagram asking Heughan — who featured in the opening ceremony — to come and watch the netball competition.

It seems their wishes may well be granted.

Loading Instagram content

We'll keep you posted on whether a meeting eventuates.

4. McCanns watch son compete

Kate and Gerry McCann watch their son Sean McCann compete in the swimming heats on day two. (Getty Images/SNS Group: Ross MacDonald)

From all reports, Kate and Gerry McCann avoided being accosted when they watched their son, Sean, compete in the men's 400m freestyle at the Tollcross International Swimming Centre.

The McCanns were the centre of a media frenzy when their three-year-old daughter Madeline went missing during a family holiday in Portugal in 2007.

It remains one of the most high-profile international missing-persons cases and is still under investigation.

The parents and Sean's twin sister, Amelie, sat in the stands for both the heats and final.

Sean McCann, who was two when Madeleine disappeared, finished fourth in his heat but snuck into the final, where he placed eighth.

5. Jersey breaks medal drought

Swimmer Filip Nowacki broke through for Jersey with his silver medal. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

The nation of Jersey has reason to celebrate after claiming its first Commonwealth Games medal in 36 years.

Filip Nowacki won silver behind Williamson in the men's 100m breaststroke final, beating world record holder Adam Ramsay-Peaty into third place.

"I'm really happy with that swim," the 18-year-old told BBC Jersey.

"It was just a touch outside my personal best, but it's a true privilege racing Adam, the Aussies and the very best in the world in a senior environment."

Nowacki's medal was only the fifth Jersey has won in Commonwealth Games history.

The last medal came at the 1990 Games in Auckland, when Colin Mallett topped the podium in the full-bore rifle.

World.title: Sobers could only do everything — including for SA's Sheffield Shield side
World.content:
The cricketer Sir Garfield St Aubrun "Garry" Sobers was a man who frequently found himself the subject of admiration and wonder.

Widely recognised as the game's greatest all-rounder, Sobers — who died recently at the age of 89 — scored 8,032 runs at an average of almost 58, claimed 235 wickets and snared 109 catches in his 93 Test matches for the West Indies.

But even by the time he was recruited by South Australia, as a 25-year-old in 1961, his talent was already indisputable.

"I don't say this lightly — he's the greatest cricketer, in my opinion, the game has ever seen," said Ken "KG" Cunningham, who played alongside Sobers during the latter's three seasons with SA's Sheffield Shield side.

"He opened the bowling, he bowled first change and bowled left arm orthodox, he was second change with left arm [wrist spin], he'd field like a demon and then he could bat.

"He was five cricketers in one."

South Australian sporting legend Ken "KG" Cunningham vividly recalls batting with Sobers. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

In 1958, Sobers had broken the world record for the highest individual innings when he scored 365 not out against Pakistan in Jamaica — a milestone that stood for more than 35 years.

His arrival in SA the summer after the famous Tied Test series occurred at a time in which there was strong enthusiasm for West Indian cricket.

"It's a little bit murky how it came about, because success always has a million fathers — but it was very much on the back of the 1960/61 West Indies tour, and I think Bradman had a role in it," sportswriter Michael Sexton said of the circumstances that led to SA securing Sobers's services.

"The lure of Bradman was just so important — they got on very well. He used to go and have dinner at Bradman's house in Adelaide."

The front cover of Michael Sexton's book Three Summers of Sobers, about Sir Garfield Sobers's time playing for SA. (Supplied)

Sexton's book Three Summers of Sobers is a tender tribute to the cricketer's SA seasons and their culmination in Sheffield Shield victory.

There are vignettes from his time at Prospect Cricket Club, where Sobers played at grade level, and the book depicts him in his off-field moments as a man who "charged past midnight, wore out barmen, gambled, chased skirts and lit every scene with the sunshine of possibility that beamed out of him".

Light is also shed on the political setting, and Sexton said South Australian administrators had "to bypass the White Australia Policy" to get Sobers into the squad.

It is an irony of considerable gravity that while Sobers was regarded by fellow cricketers as having reached the summit of their sport, cricket authorities were obliged to seek, with delicacy and discretion, special dispensation to keep him in the country.

'So grateful and so lucky'

In person, there was nothing immediately imposing about Sobers, and little to indicate that his frame concealed an inner Hercules. The short back and sides, the pencil moustache and the V-neck sweater hardly betokened the presence of athletic genius.

But Sobers was, in truth, a cricketer of whom it feels apt to borrow a bon mot: he could only do everything.

The paradoxical presence of the word "only" in that statement adds the crucial note of humility that makes it especially applicable to Sobers, whose accomplishments were usually accompanied by grace.

The news that Sobers was destined for SA generated headlines across Australia. (Supplied)

In one of his six sixes in an over for Nottinghamshire at Swansea in 1968, he performed a complete pirouette, spinning like a sprinkler on a parched outfield.

His bowling action was equally aqueous. The rock back and forward sling prefigured the motions of Jeff Thomson, and the ball was released in a cascade of lithe force.

"He was the best player in the world — and he's just turning up at Prospect to go and have a net with the others, because he was in that team," Sexton said.

"It's an astonishing thing that happened to South Australia. It's probably the equivalent of when Bradman came in the 1930s — it's that sort of impact, isn't it? 'What on Earth is he doing here?'"

For his Prospect teammates, the experience was perhaps not unlike that of an amateur dramatic society that persuades a BAFTA-winning lead to join its players, or a garage band that fills the vacant role of rhythm guitarist by recruiting a rock legend, or a model aeroplane club that without warning is gifted possession of an actual Spitfire.

But Sobers's career in South Australia had unpropitious beginnings, and his initial three outings with the bat for Prospect produced a solitary run.

A team photo of the South Australian 1963/64 Sheffield Shield side, including Ken Cunningham, Neil Hawke, Sir Garfield Sobers, Rex Sellers, Les Favell, Barry Jarman and Ian Chappell. (Supplied)

Even so, his cricketing charisma was palpable, and Cunningham still remembers the first time they batted together for SA.

"I walked down the beautiful steps at Adelaide Oval, onto the oval itself, and went to the striker's end," he said.

"I looked up and I saw Sir Garfield Sobers [at the other end] and I said to myself, 'What in the hell am I doing here? I'm just Ken Cunningham. I shouldn't be here'.

"I was so grateful and so lucky to be able to play with the great man."

Sobers's seasons in SA were like the building and breaking of a wave, and triumph came in 1963/64.

A newspaper  from around the time of Sobers's remarkable achievement in the 1963/64 Sheffield Shield season. (Supplied)

Remarkably, he took more wickets and scored more runs than any player in Australia during the summer.

Among the mainstays of that Shield victory was the bowling partnership Sobers formed with leg-spinner Rex Sellers — the former took 47 wickets, the latter 46.

"I s'pose we might have complemented each other," Sellers reflected.

"He was very accurate, I believe I can say I was pretty accurate as well, so we created good pressure on batsmen from both ends."

In SA's final game — a win against Victoria that guaranteed SA the Shield — Sobers made a century and claimed nine scalps.

"He was pivotal because not only was he the best player, but he inspired the others to play better. He gave them a slight swagger and a confidence that they hadn't had before," Sexton said.

"He lived up to all expectations and hopes."

World.title: Pogačar on the cusp of Tour history after dramatic penultimate stage
World.content:
Tadej Pogačar moved to within touching distance of a record-equalling fifth Tour de France title after finishing safely in the penultimate stage overnight.

The Slovenian star heads into tonight's showcase finish in Paris with a lead of six and a half minutes over Belgian rider Remco Evenepoel.

Barring mishap, Pogačar will join Belgian Eddy Merckx, Spaniard Miguel Indurain, and Frenchmen Jacques Anquetil and Bernard Hinault as the only men to win five Tours.

"I have done a really good Tour. Some of our competitors had bad luck," said Pogačar, whose main rival Jonas Vingegaard crashed out of the race.

"We made it through with the team and now there is just one last show left."

The 20th stage was won by Richard Carapaz for his second win at this year's race and third overall. The Ecuadorian rider overtook Sepp Kuss near the end as the American almost crashed out. Evenepoel also surged past Kuss near the line to take second place.

"There was a moment when I couldn't believe what was happening," Carapaz said.

"This Tour de France has been incredible, with all the spectators and all the support I've received from Ecuador, where they'll be jumping for joy."

Pogačar chose not to launch one of his attacks like on Friday's 19th stage.

Stage 20 was a mammoth 171-kilometre alpine trek featuring three hors catégorie climbs, the hardest category, and one category 1 climb.

After three weeks in the saddle, weary riders tackled hors catégorie ascents of Col de la Croix de Fer, Col du Galibier and Col de Sarenne, and the one category 1 climb of Col du Télégraphe, making for 66km of hard climbing in total before a hilly finish to Alpe d'Huez.

Carapaz rode from the front to secure the polka-dot jersey awarded to the Tour's best climber. Pogacar's yellow jersey group was hanging back when Carapaz, Kuss, Spaniard Juan Ayuso and Australian Jai Hindley went over the Galibier together.

Pogačar's priority was ensuring his AE Team Emirates teammate Isaac Del Toro finished third in the rankings, and the Mexican rider is now more than two minutes clear of Frenchman Paul Seixas in fourth.

"It's been an honour to ride for Isaac today," said Pogačar, who gifted Del Toro victory on Stage 2.

"Crossing the finish line together with him has been memorable."

Ayuso was dropped as the former Spanish Vuelta winner Kuss, Hindley and Carapaz — both former Giro d'Italia winners — battled for supremacy in the Sarenne pass.

"It was really, really tough," Carapaz said.

"Sepp, in particular, was a very tough nut to crack."

An exhausted-looking Kuss lost control of his bike going downhill when he mistimed a turn with 5km left and almost tumbled over a roadside concrete barrier. Some netting cushioned him.

Carapaz rode swiftly past him to victory.

"It was absolutely brilliant to win here and in a distinctive jersey," Carapaz said.

"I think I deserve it, because I've fought so hard in this Tour de France."

Pogačar has won five stages on this year's race and 26 overall, meaning he would likely need to compete in at least two more Tours to beat British sprinter Mark Cavendish's record of 35 stage wins. Merckx won 34 and Hinault 28.

He may go for another stage win tonight.

"Let's see how I feel tomorrow. I won't take any risks," Pogačar said.

"But if I have good legs and I don't have to take too many big risks, I'll try to claim victory tomorrow."

The final stage is on an 89km route featuring an uphill dash through the Montmartre district in Paris and finishing on the Champs-Élysées.

The stage was shortened from 133km and its starting point in Thoiry, west of the capital, was changed to Paris to reduce pressure on emergency services combating wildfires in the south-west.

World.title: Aussies won't allow anticipated clash with English defector to distract them
World.content:
Most elite athletes not named Michael Jordan don't need to make things personal to perform at their peak, and that's certainly the case for Leigh Hoffman.

And he wouldn't have to look far for personal animus if he wanted to find some.

The last time the Australian track cycling team was competing in Glasgow, at the 2023 world championships, and the last time he was at the Commonwealth Games, at Birmingham 2022, he was alongside Matthew Richardson.

In fact, the first four major medals of Hoffman's career came in team sprints with Richardson, including bronze at the 2024 Paris Olympics.

But then, as Hoffman told it on his arrival in Glasgow, they "brought a few medals back for Australia and then he went on holiday and never came back".

Leigh Hoffman, Matthew Richardson and Matthew Glaetzer are the reigning Commonwealth Games gold medallists in the men's team sprint. (Getty Images: John Walton/PA Images)

Richardson defected to the country of his birth after the Games and will ride for England at the Commonwealth Games for the first time.

On the way out, he took a few shots at the apparently insufficient Cycling Australia program, with whom he won 10 medals across Olympics, world champs and Commonwealth Games.

"We'd never experienced something like that," Hoffman said.

"You grow up racing with someone and you think you're both Aussies and then he's not. That's life. It is what it is."

Leigh Hoffman and co went through a lot with Richardson (centre). (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Hoffman's cavalier attitude to the impossibly hyped rivalry with Richardson ahead of a potential team sprint final clash next Friday morning makes sense for a couple of reasons.

Firstly, the format of track cycling being so cutthroat, these guys are no strangers to racing each other anyway.

"We'd be racing with each other in the team sprint, and every other event you race as an individual anyway," Hoffman said.

Richardson breaks WR — for Great Britain A year after winning Olympic silver for Australia, Matthew Richardson has become the fastest cyclist of all-time — in the colours of Great Britain.

"So even if he still represented Australia, I'd still have to come against my own teammate and aim to try and beat him and he'd be aiming to try and beat me.

"It's kinda life in track cycling."

The other reason is the amount of turnover across the team.

In addition to Richardson's defection, five-time Commonwealth gold medallist Matthew Glaetzer retired, and Tom Cornish pivoted to the endurance events.

Hoffman has suddenly gone from the young buck at the Birmingham Games to the leader of a new-look sprint unit, with 23-year-old Danny Barber, 22-year-old Ryan Elliott, and 20-year-old Tayte Ryan.

The Aussies have been competing against Richardson relatively amicably the past few years. (Getty Images: Matt Jelonek)

They will relish beating England, but will not be focusing too much on Richardson, because if you're looking the wrong way on the bike, you can easily get passed on your blind side.

"I'm excited to beat everyone in the world, he's just another domino to fall, hopefully," Hoffman said.

"The Australia-England rivalry goes back very far with the Ashes and all our other sports. It's always Australia vs England, [but] for the Commonwealth Games, we've got some really stacked riders.

"Azizul Awang from Malaysia, who's come in in great form; Trinidad and Tobago, Nicholas Paul – there's a lot of great riders.

"But the fans are definitely looking forward to an Australia-England match-up."

Tech.title: The vertical video takeover is here
Tech.content:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on all things vertical video, follow David Pierce. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

For a while, every social and media platform had its own identity. YouTube was for clips of TV shows and movies, and the home of so many members of a burgeoning creator community. Instagram was mostly pictures. Netflix was trying to be the on-demand HBO. Facebook was about friends. Twitter was about news. Snapchat was a messaging app.

All these apps did have one important thing in common, though: They were growing up alongside the smartphone. Billions of new people were coming online for the first time, and they began to make content that made sense for the tall, skinny new devices in their hands. Selfies were a vertical art form, both because the photos filled the screen better and because it was just easier to hold the phone and take the photo that way. Some resisted the idea of vertical video for years — they’d argue that our eyes are meant to scan horizontally rather than vertically, and that vertical video looked bad on widescreen laptops. But ultimately phones won, and we hold our phones upright, so our phone experiences turned upright. That includes entertainment.

As has been true so many times, Snap figured this out before anyone. It launched Stories in late 2013 as a slightly more relaxed way to see what your friends are up to. CEO Evan Spiegel called it a “totally new way to share your day with friends — or everyone.” It took off in a massive way, and by the middle of 2014 was the most popular feature on Snapchat. That’s the kind of virality that Mark Zuckerberg tends to notice, and by August of 2016, the feature had been copied more or less exactly into Instagram. Kevin Systrom, then the CEO of Instagram, said of Spiegel and Snapchat that “they deserve all the credit” for Stories. The implication? That this was no longer a proprietary feature of a single social network; it was just in the air. Stories were for everyone. They started showing up on LinkedIn, Tinder, Medium, and so many other places.

Stories weren’t always video, but as cameras and upload speeds improved, video became the dominant medium in many ephemeral spaces. And video stories had two semi-magical properties: They were perfectly suited to endless, mindless scrolling, and they made it really easy to integrate ads. Only a few months after turning on Stories in Instagram, by which point half the platform’s users were already using Stories, Facebook began flooding ads into the product. The semi-randomness of Stories made ads actually seem less intrusive — you’d see a photo of a dog, a video of a hike, an ad for jeans, your friend’s makeup routine, brunch pics, an ad for blush. Video ads felt more premium, took up the whole screen, and were thus far more lucrative for the social platforms.

With apologies to the short, brilliant life of Vine, the six-second video platform that helped invent so much about the video-first social network, it wasn’t until TikTok took off that things really turned again. The platform launched in the US in 2018, but had been popular for a few years in China as Douyin and elsewhere as Musical.ly. TikTok combined the vertical-first format of Stories with the permanence of YouTube, but it also made video easier than ever. It had filters like Instagram and Snapchat, but also supplied a steady stream of video ideas through the platform’s many trends, offered access to music and sound effects, and made it easy to stitch or duet a video.

By defaulting to the purely algorithmic For You page, TikTok also freed creators from caring about curating their profile or worrying about posting too much — you could just pump out videos and trust the algorithm to deliver them. And so that’s what people did. Pretty quickly, TikTok became one of the fastest growing apps on the planet, and its daily usage numbers became the envy of the industry. Instagram may have had more users, but TikTok users spent far more time TikToking.

When TikTok became a phenomenon, just about everyone jumped on the vertical video bandwagon. Reels launched in 2020 and became a core feature of both Instagram and Facebook; YouTube created Shorts a year later. By the end of 2021, Twitter had both launched and killed a similar feature called Fleets. By this point, this kind of full-screen, vertical-scrolling video was part of the lingua franca of the smartphone. At the same time, in a search for ever more engagement, these platforms were learning another lesson from TikTok: to stop relying on your friends to post interesting content, and instead to show you whatever the algorithm thinks you might like. Social networks were gone, replaced by social media — entertainment with a comments section.

How it’s going

Short-form, vertical video has effectively won the internet. Business is booming, and viewers show no sign of tuning out. Meta said in 2024 that Instagram users were spending more than half their time in Reels, and said in 2025 the feature was turning into a $50 billion annual business across Meta’s apps. About 63 percent of young adults and teens are on TikTok, per Pew Research Center, and one in five teens reported being on the app “almost constantly.” YouTube reported 200 billion daily views of Shorts at the end of 2025, and said that Shorts earned more money per watch hour than standard YouTube videos.

The last three or four years have been about relentless standardization in social media. The pace with which these products copy each other, and regress back toward parity, has been absolutely astonishing. First, Shorts and Reels both aped TikTok’s design, its duetting and stitching, and its close relationship with sounds and music. Then they bought into TikTok’s idea of prioritizing content over connection — followers are dead, long live the algorithm. TikTok pushed hard into shopping, then suddenly Reels and Shorts became a lot more shoppable. YouTube began to grow on TVs, and suddenly TikTok and Instagram started investing in its own TV apps. Videos got longer and longer across platforms, to allow more ads. All the apps got really into livestreaming for a while. And micro dramas. They’ve relentlessly copied each other on big things like letting users control their algorithm, and small things like Clear Mode.

There are two reasons for the ongoing onslaught of short-form vertical video: time spent and advertising. The endlessly scrolling video feed turns out to be one of the most engrossing forms of entertainment ever devised (to the point that it has become a regulatory problem for the social platforms), and in a relentless competition for eyeballs and attention, it has become everyone’s best idea. In 2024, when Meta switched its default video player to a vertical-first layout across all platforms, the race was officially won.

Meanwhile, as those platforms have captured more of our time and attention, short-form video has become a dominant force of advertising on the internet, which means advertisers are already comfortable making ads designed to go between videos in the feed. And as so many companies turn to AI to do their ad targeting, all they really need is the creative to get started. “So long as clients give us different assets — a six-second ad, a 15-second ad, a long-format, a vertical ad — AI is essentially powering everything else,” YouTube’s Brian Albert told me last year. “From the audiences you’re reaching, to the contextual placements, to the ad that’s actually showing.” The combination of AI and vertical video has become a self-fulfilling prophecy: The more it wins, the easier it becomes for everyone else to get on board, and so it just keeps winning.

What happens next

Vertical video haters, I have bad news: It’s only going to get worse. TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram are if anything going to become more short-form and vertical, since those short videos are easier to make and easier to load into endlessly scrolling feeds. Video services used to require you to pick something and press play, but now all they need is for you to open the app and they can start showing you ads. They’re not going to want to go back. Here’s how dominant video is: Facebook is testing a new version of the app that loads a full-screen video feed when you open the app. If that happens, there will be no Facebook — only Reels. After all this time, they’ve trained users to want and expect this kind of fast-paced, instant-gratification entertainment, to the point where even a full-length movie can feel like a chore.

Meanwhile, after years of raising prices, streaming services around the world are hoping they can turn to advertising to keep growing. For a while, they could coast on the back of linear TV, borrowing those ads to run on digital platforms. But a TikTok ad won’t make any sense on Netflix, so Netflix decided the best thing to do is build something that looks more like TikTok. A recent HubSpot report found that short-form video was by a wide margin both the most-used and most successful form of marketing content in 2025, and that it was the format in which marketers planned to invest the most this year.

All that said, there are glimmers of a bigger shift beginning to happen. Fed up with the algorithm, some users are starting to demand the return of friends and family in social media. But more broadly, more and more young people are deciding to put down their phones, resist the invasion of AI into their lives, and look for different kinds of entertainment. Movie theaters are having a big year; one of the year’s most exciting new phones is a flip phone. As long as we live in this era of social media and entertainment, vertical video is going to win. It would take a cultural revolution to stop it — and there might just be one brewing.

By the way

The best way to understand TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat in particular right now is as a combination of two things: a streaming service and an inbox. Studies have found that the most popular thing to do is watch videos, and the second most popular thing is to send videos to someone else. Actually posting? Way down the list. (YouTube, by the way, is desperately trying to make DMs happen .)

If you’ve made it this far and you’re thinking, no way, you’re way overstating it? I’m so sorry to say this, but you might just be old. At this point, YouTube and Facebook cross generations and demographics, but Pew and others have found that TikTok, Snapchat, and Instagram are effectively ubiquitous among young people in particular.

It’s important to remember that views are lies . Everyone on the internet has an incentive to make their platform seem big and vibrant and popular, and they will invent whatever new metrics they need to do so.
